articles.title: Google says it fixed more Chrome bugs in June than over the past two years, thanks to AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As experts have warned for the last two years, some companies — like Microsoft and now Google — are finding and patching an exponential number of bugs in their products, thanks to the use of LLMs and AI tools.
articles.body:
With help from its internal AI tools, Google says it has patched more security flaws in its Chrome browser in the last month than in the past two years combined.

The tech giant announced on Thursday that it has fixed a whopping 1,072 security bugs in the last two versions of Chrome, both released in June. That is more than the number of bugs patched in the previous 23 versions released over the last two years, which totaled 1,036 fixes.

Ever since the advent of LLMs, cybersecurity experts have warned that AI-powered systems would find an increasingly and exponentially enormous amount of bugs, forcing defenders to also use AI to get ahead of malicious hackers.

That prediction is starting to come true, and it’s backed by real data.

A chart published by Google, which the company revealed as part of a white paper on the company’s efforts to use AI to find flaws and patch them faster, shows the exponential increase. For context, Chrome’s 126 was released in June 2024, while the latest two Chrome releases, Chrome 149 and 150, were released last month. Google calls each version a “milestone.”

Doug Turner, Chrome’s director of engineering, told TechCrunch in a statement that LLMs have “fundamentally shifted the economics of cybersecurity, transforming vulnerability discovery into an automated, industrial-scale operation.”

“By applying models like Gemini, we are preemptively fixing vulnerabilities, outpacing our adversaries and making Chrome safer with every update,” said Turner.

Google is not the only company seeing this trend.

Earlier this month, Microsoft announced that it had patched a record 570 security flaws across its product lines as part of its monthly round of scheduled patches — colloquially known as “Patch Tuesday.” Microsoft cited its own use of AI to explain the sudden jump in bug fixes.

Apple, meanwhile, does not appear to be registering the same exponential increase. According to an independent count of bugs fixed in its products, Apple has patched 482 bugs in 2026, which is roughly on pace to equal or surpass the number of fixed bugs from last year, and also roughly equal from the number of bugs that Apple patched in 2015.

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment, but did not hear back.

articles.title: Nvidia doesn't mess around: A week after open AI industry group formed, it's already showing progress | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The week-old Open Secure AI Alliance, spearheaded by Nvidia and grown to over 120 companies, already has proposals out for defending against AI agents.
articles.body:
The week-old Open Secure AI Alliance (OSAA), an industry group spearheaded by Nvidia that has already grown to over 120 companies, has developed a cutely named working group, the Shared AI Findings Exchange, or SAFE. The group is already presenting proposals for open comment, and the Linux Foundation, a member of the group, is managing the proposals.

The group developed them while members gathered at the nexus of the cybersecurity world, the Black Hat conference, taking place this week in Las Vegas.

articles.title: Ring upgraded its peephole doorbell camera to 2K
articles.summary: Ring’s new Peephole Cam 2K smart doorbell camera gets a big resolution upgrade and a price drop to $100.
articles.body: Ring has debuted a new version of its smart doorbell camera that’s designed to be easily installed as a replacement for a door’s peephole without drilling or running wires. The Peephole Cam 2K is a replacement for the brand’s Door View Cam that first debuted in 2019 and, alongside a sleeker design, it features a bump from 1080P to 2K video recording, some tracking upgrades, and a cheaper price. It’s available for preorder now for $99.99 with shipping expected later this month. As with previous models, the Peephole Cam 2K is divided into two halves that connect to each other through your door’s peephole. On the outside there’s a camera, doorbell, speaker, and microphone, while inside are additional electronics including a removable battery good for an estimated 120 days of use between charges. But there’s no preview screen on the inside, so to check who’s at your door you’ll need to reach for your phone or a compatible smart display. [Image: The two halves of the camera connect through a door’s peephole, so no drilling or complicated wiring is required. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ring2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That inconvenience is potentially outweighed by being able to see and respond to whoever’s at your door from anywhere, even when you’re not at home. The Peephole Cam 2K will also deliver real-time motion alerts with brief descriptions of what its camera is seeing, and you can limit its motion detection to specific regions of its wide-angle 140-degree field-of-view so that passing cars, for example, don’t trigger alerts. However, features like being able to review recorded events for up to 180 days and specific alerts for detected packages are only available with an additional Ring Protect plan.

articles.title: Google says hackers are calling financial firm employees to hack and extort victims | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Groups of hackers are breaking into large U.S. financial firms to steal sensitive data and extort victims, Google’s security researchers report.
articles.body:
Even in the age of AI-powered autonomous cyberattacks , the crude, tried and tested hacking techniques of tricking victims into doing things they shouldn’t are still producing great results.

Groups of unknown hackers are targeting and breaking into large financial and investment firms in the United States with the goal of stealing sensitive data to extort the victims with the threat of publishing it, Google’s security researchers wrote in a report on Thursday.

The company did not name the victims, but Reuters reported that among them there are leading private equity firms such as Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, CME Group, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG.

The hacking groups, which Google dubbed Falcon, Helix, Pink, and Redact, are using an old-fashioned technique to break into those firms: phone calls to employees’ personal cellphones in which the hackers pretend to be co-workers or IT helpdesk staffers, during which they try to trick targets into entering their credentials and multi-factor codes on spoofed websites, according to Google. In cybersecurity parlance, this technique is known as voice phishing, or vishing.

Some of the groups identified by Google run websites where they publicize their hacks and threaten to leak the stolen data as a way to extort the victims into paying a ransom, a common strategy among cybercriminals.

“We conduct every negotiation on professional terms. The publication of your data is never our preferred resolution; it is the consequence of refusal to engage, deliberate stalling, or failure to honor an agreement,” read one of the sites. “Respond promptly and in good faith, and the matter is resolved without further incident.”

Google researchers said that the different groups may all be part of a larger umbrella collective the company tracks under the name UNC6671. But it’s unclear if they are affiliates, splinter groups, or they all use the same Phishing-as-a-Service infrastructure.

“We believe that this most likely reflects a coordinated group of threat actors operating multiple public extortion brands possibly in an effort to compartmentalize operations, hide overall breach volumes, and isolate any negotiation fallout,” read the report.

According to Google, the hacking groups have also previously targeted large companies in the manufacturing, real estate, healthcare, and insurance sectors, as well as tech, transportation, and hospitality companies with the goal of stealing “valuable intellectual property, software source code, or sensitive VIP client data.”

More recently, the hackers have targeted legal and financial organizations such as private equity firms. “Concentrating on organizations involved in mergers, acquisitions, capital deployment, and litigation may reflect a strategy to target high-value corporate and confidential data to maximize leverage extortion demands,” wrote Google’s researchers.

Google said that one cryptocurrency wallet associated with one of the hacking groups received around $10 million in bitcoin in the first few months of this year, and that the hackers usually demand from $750,000 to $3 million from victims.

Laurie Bischel, a spokesperson for CME Group, declined to comment.

Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Google's top hacker hunter explains why hacking groups get code names | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google recently changed how it refers and assigns names to hacking groups. TechCrunch spoke with one of the world’s foremost experts on tracking hackers to understand why companies give hackers codenames.
articles.body:
For more than a decade, the cybersecurity industry has been assigning names to different hacking groups. Some of them, like Fancy Bear , have crossed over into the mainstream because of their prominent hacks and memorable names. Others are only known within the cybersecurity industry.

Oftentimes, even industry insiders can’t keep track. In part, that’s because every company names hacking groups differently. That’s why there are resources like this one , which attempt to be a one-stop shop where cybersecurity professionals, government officials, policymakers, journalists, and the wider public can make sense of who is who.

Last month, Google became the latest company to revamp its naming system for hacking groups.

Gone are the days of APT1, APT41, or APT whatever number , which was the system adopted by Mandiant, once an independent security firm that’s now part of Google. Mandiant was the first to adopt a naming scheme.

From now on, Google’s system is relatively simple: A hacking group will have a first name that is memorable and random, and a second word whose initial indicates the country of origin: Castle for China, Ion for Iran, Neptune for North Korea, and Relic for Russia.

According to Shane Huntley, the chief technology officer of Google Threat Intelligence Group, the company’s in-house hacker hunting team, the revamp was necessary to bring clarity to security researchers both inside the company and externally.

In the early 2010s, when companies started publishing reports on cyberattacks and naming the hackers behind them, Huntley told TechCrunch, “We were not expecting to have as many threat groups as we do today.”

It became hard to keep track of everyone. Google now tracks more than 5,000 “activity clusters” in several countries, according to John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group. Huntley said that there are very few developed nations that don’t have their own cyber capabilities and hacking groups.

But what is the point of naming hacking groups? It’s not just an academic exercise, Huntley explained. The goal is to have a baseline understanding of who is attacking who, and how they are attacking them. That way organizations can recognize threats more quickly, prepare against them, and ideally stop them, or at least investigate incidents more promptly.

All that, he said, is possible only if you name the hackers and track them consistently.

“If you actually get hacked by them or you’re dealing with some incident, knowing how that actor behaves, what they do, what they’ve done in the past, all of these details become critically important to help the response and also work out your coverage against these threats as well,” said Huntley.

Knowing how the North Korean government hackers known as the Lazarus Group behave, what their goals usually are, and who they work for gives defenders a starting point in dealing with these hackers.

Tracking state-sponsored hackers, while challenging, is easier than tracking cybercriminal groups and hackers-for-hire, Huntley explained. The government hackers tend to have more consistent targets and activities, while cybercriminal groups have members that come and go, sometimes splinter, and otherwise are more amorphous. Hacker-for-hire groups and spyware makers tend to have a lot of customers in different parts of the world, making them slightly harder to track.

A common criticism whenever a new naming system gets announced is: Why don’t all companies and organizations just use the same code names? While that seems like an easy question to answer, the reality is that every company has a slightly different view of every group, based on their own sets of data and telemetry. Huntley said this is an inescapable reality that can’t be avoided just by sharing more information among companies and groups of researchers.

“No one has perfect visibility,” he said. “We are building our model and our best understanding, but we will never know everything about what’s going on.”

By unifying the naming scheme of Google’s old Threat Analysis Group, which Huntley headed, and Mandiant, at least now there’s one fewer scheme to remember. For everything else, refer to this gargantuan list .

articles.title: Brendan Carr is one firing away from an unchecked FCC
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s nomination of Republican Danielle Thumann Severs to the Federal Communications Commission raises questions about the agency’s rules.
articles.body: President Donald Trump already holds a Republican majority in the agency tasked with regulating America’s communications systems. But with a new nomination to the Federal Communications Commission, he could move to shut out opposing voices altogether — albeit at a legal risk. The FCC is currently composed of two Republicans and one Democrat — Republican Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, and Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez. This mixed group gives the agency a three-member quorum that allows it to vote on major actions, though it still falls short of the five members (no more than three from a single party) the FCC is meant to have. But late last week, Trump nominated a third Republican, Carr adviser Danielle Thumann Severs. If she’s confirmed, it won’t change the basic math of which policies win votes. But it would mean there’s a quorum even without Gomez. That could open the door to Trump firing the FCC’s lone Democrat, something she herself has wondered why he hasn’t already done. Gomez may not have much hard power in the current FCC, but her removal would be a blow to the public interest. Commissioners often have access to information that the public might not otherwise know about, and can raise nonconfidential issues in their public dissents and statements. And even in situations where dissenting voices are overruled, they can push the majority to offer more robust reasoning in their decisions. During the Trump administration, Gomez has used her post to call attention to FCC actions she thinks violate the First Amendment, and pushed back on policies loosening broadcast consolidation rules. Even with Gomez in place, Carr’s FCC has threatened broadcasters over programming they air under seldom-used rules, approved a major broadcast merger by waiving policies set by Congress, and banned Roombas.  Trump could well be able to remove Gomez, given that he fired the Federal Trade Commission’s two Democrats without cause and got away with it. Like the FTC, the FCC was created as an independent agency, with a bipartisan panel of staggered terms that would supposedly insulate it from a given administration’s whims. But under the unitary executive theory, which Trump allies including Carr and FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson endorse, all power held by them belongs to the president. The Supreme Court’s ruling affirming Trump’s ability to fire the FTC’s Democrats bolstered this. But there are still good reasons Trump could spare Gomez, particularly that firing her could put the FCC’s legitimacy in question, as former FCC senior staffer Blair Levin writes. Even after SCOTUS legitimized the FTC firings, the Communications Act’s language grants the FCC unique quirks. It could provide stronger legal ground to argue that one party can’t hold all the seats on the panel, Levin adds, and a court could determine it is more like the Federal Reserve, insulated from presidential firings, than the FTC.  Gomez’ term is technically lapsed, but she can stay on until the end of 2027 unless her seat is filled sooner, or she’s renominated. With limited Senate floor time ahead of the midterm elections and key Democrats’ opposition to confirming a Republican nominee without a Democratic one, the FCC could remain in a holding pattern for quite some time.

articles.title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
articles.summary: Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android.
articles.body: One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android. It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complete access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years. But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them. First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed. [Image: These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/app-store-changes-google-play.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen. Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted. “Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so. Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page. That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal app store search results. Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked. Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water. “We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and 10 things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for. “Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said. The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘
paragraphs: One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android. It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complete access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years. But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them. First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed. [Image: These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/app-store-changes-google-play.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen. Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted. “Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so. Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page. That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal app store search results. Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked. Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water. “We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and 10 things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for. “Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said. The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

articles.title: Apple and Epic argue over how much Apple should get from purchases made outside the App Store
articles.summary: Apple’s new App Store proposal would allow it to collect fees from developers on digital purchases made via external links, including a 15 percent cut from standard apps.
articles.body: In a new filing in its long-running legal dispute with Epic Games, Apple has proposed a structure that would allow it to collect fees on digital purchases made via external links that don’t use the company’s in-app purchase system. Epic has already responded, saying that Apple’s request is “far outside of the bounds” of the court’s guidance. Right now, Apple cannot take a commission on external purchases after California district court judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in April 2025 that the company “willfully” didn’t comply with her 2021 Epic Games v. Apple injunction. However, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel said that Apple should be able to charge a commission based on “necessary costs,” and Apple shared its proposal for fees in Thursday’s filing. (The Supreme Court has also said it will hear arguments about whether Apple willfully violated the April 2025 ruling.) Under Apple’s proposal, it would collect: * 15 percent of fees from purchases in “standard apps” * 10 percent of fees for apps in the Video Partner Program, the News Partner Program, the Mini Apps Partner Program, and subscription renewals * 5 percent of fees from apps in the Small Business Program However, Apple says its “necessary costs” to allow external purchases, as defined by the Ninth Circuit, “would be essentially zero.” The company argues that, based on an “expert analysis,” at the proposed rates, “it appears that large numbers of U.S. developers collectively accounting for the lion’s share of App Store revenue will be able to link out profitably.” Apple also says the rates would let it recoup “at least some compensation” for its tools, technologies, and services it provides to developers. Here’s Epic’s statement in reply to the filing: > Apple’s filing is in, and Apple admitted that under the Ninth Circuit’s definition of “necessary costs” they would charge 0% for purchases made via linkouts to the web. > Apple proposed linkout fees of 15% for standard apps and 5% for Small Business Program apps. Epic believes these fees are far outside of the bounds of the Ninth Circuit’s guidance on permissible fees, and we have roughly 60 days to file our opposition supported by expert witnesses.

articles.title: Trump declares 100 percent tariffs on many drones and all aircraft parts
articles.summary: President Trump has declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of aircraft weighing over 25kg.
articles.body: The United States has already banned future foreign drones from entering the United States unless their companies kiss the ring — as well as routers, robots, and Roombas. Now, President Donald Trump is targeting existing drone imports and parts, too. He’s going to try to make them cost a lot more. In a presidential action, he’s declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of unmanned aircraft weighing over 25kg — you can read the full list here. For all other drones, including tiny sub-250-gram “Mini” consumer drones, he’s declared a 25 percent tariff. In Trump fashion, these tariffs have a huge loophole: If a company commits to making some of their drones or aircraft parts in the United States, they don’t have to pay tariffs. Trump suggested he’d make similar deals when he threatened a 100 percent tariff on computer chips last year. And Trump is giving the EU, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan a lower rate of 15 percent, and a rate of 10 percent for the UK, “provided that substantially all hardware, software, and technology originates from within these countries and the United States.” Stated reasons for the new tariffs include: * “many U.S. commercial manufacturers that produce UAS domestically are highly dependent on foreign sources for critical UAS components, such as motors, electronic speed controllers, lithium-ion batteries, and docking stations, which creates unacceptable national security vulnerabilities.” * “products pose an information technology security risk because their software allows data to be sent back to the manufacturer in a foreign country.” * “there are concerns as to whether the U.S. industry can produce UAS and UAS components at the required speed and scale to adequately support national security operations and activities, including during a surge for wartime or armed conflict, or in a manner to sustain long-term economic competitiveness.” Trump is also dangling a carrot, not just wielding a stick. The proclamation states that he’s authorizing the Secretary of Commerce to create a new program “to incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce UAS and UAS components.” That could be interesting, but last we checked, the government’s drone incentives were aimed toward drones for war. The Supreme Court already ruled earlier this year that Trump’s global tariffs were illegal; the US Court of International Trade ruled against them too, though Trump continues to announce more. As of today, it appears that Trump’s tariffs are enriching corporate America at the expense of everyday citizens. First, companies raise their prices so that you pay the cost of tariffs instead of them. Then, those companies get gigantic refunds from the government when the tariffs are declared illegal. Finally, they profit. Companies do not pass those refunds along to you, even though you paid for them, and they do not lower their prices either. The tariffs aren’t the US government’s only attempt to target larger foreign drones in the US. The FCC recently threatened to retroactively ban “military-grade” drones using definitions that would also catch drones for farmers, first responders, and light shows in the same net.

articles.title: Judge orders Kalshi to shut down most of its bets in Washington.
articles.summary:
A preliminary injunction issued Wednesday finds the prediction market has likely broken state laws against running an illegal gambling operation.
Washington State AG Nick Brown:
> The order requires Kalshi to stop offering, accepting, or facilitating wagers on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions in Washington. Kalshi must implement an IP address and residency based geofence by August 19 and a multi-source geofencing solution by September 2.
> This does not include all the wagers offered on Kalshi, but it includes a substantial part of their business, which in recent years has been increasingly driven by sports wagers.

articles.title: When housing is unaffordable, this artist’s device makes pedaling harder
articles.summary: Brooklyn-based artist Justin Blinder created a device that illustrates how soaring housing costs are making life in the city that much harder.
articles.body: Justin Blinder had just been laid off when he first came up with the idea for Ground Truth. It was 2020, two weeks before covid lockdown went into effect, and the Brooklyn-based artist and technologist had no idea what the future would hold. He started working for the food delivery apps, and as he was riding his bike across the city, he began noticing the stark differences between neighborhoods. “I really started to kind of become a bit more aware of how different neighborhoods, often right next to each other, could feel very economically and psychologically very far apart, even though it’s just really within close proximity,” he said. “And also just how those inequalities can sometimes feel quite unusually physical. A lot of times higher elevation can contribute to the desirability and cost of a neighborhood through better views and lower flood exposure.” These observations led him to think about the relationship between the food he was delivering, the neighborhoods it was going to, the buildings he encountered, and even the expectations he developed about potential tips. “All that kind of culminated into this sort of line of thinking that led to Ground Truth that had been percolating after that for a few years,” Blinder said. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-connection.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-field-04.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-03.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Ground Truth, Blinder’s new art project, is a small gray box that attaches to the front fork of a bike and changes the physical difficulty of riding according to the housing affordability of the surrounding neighborhood. When housing is more affordable, pedaling becomes easier. But when a rider enters an area where housing costs consume a larger proportion of residents’ incomes, the bike’s resistance increases, making the rider work harder. “And so it’s really thinking about how to take economic abstractions in this case, really the affordability of cost-of-living prices, and turn them from something that really reduces people to numbers and brings it back into more of a direct physical experience that’s rooted in reality and in the streets,” he said. After abandoning some early ideas for fear of unexpected legal consequences, Blinder settled on building an external mechanism that would allow him to affect the bike without penetrating its closed electronic systems. Using a Citi Bike as his “canvas,” he noticed that the front drum-brake mechanism was physically exposed. When the rider pulls the front brake handle, a lever on the front fork moves to apply pressure. He realized he could build a wireless mechanism that attaches to this lever and effectively acts as an additional brake actuator, allowing the device to increase or decrease the bike’s resistance. The hardware itself is relatively simple, consisting of an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, a GPS module, a high-torque servo motor capable of precisely controlling its rotation, and an SD card reader for storing the data set locally. To be sure, the device doesn’t log a rider’s location or transmit data; everything operates offline. “I’d say the harder part is actually just building an enclosure that fit perfectly onto the frame that you could just slip on without any additional hardware,” Blinder said. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-components-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-circuit-schematic.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-device-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ground-truth-mainboard.png?quality=90&strip=all] The issue of finding the right housing data to use turned out to be the real challenge. He eventually settled on using the US government’s American Community Survey’s Rent Burden dataset, so as to accurately capture the proportion of a household’s income that was being put toward rent and utilities. Blinder said he uses two measures: the median share of income spent on rent and the percentage of renting households that spend at least half of their income on housing. He then assigns each census block group a value corresponding to the amount of brake tension the device should apply there. Then he took it for a test ride. He found that riding through neighborhoods with a lot of public housing, such as apartment buildings managed by the city’s NYCHA housing agency, the bike would go faster. Meanwhile, some luxury towers are legally required to have affordable apartments, which can complicate the picture presented by those opposed to their construction. His Ground Truth project was already producing surprising results. “So it is sometimes really hard to tell what is affordable, what isn’t,” he said. Blinder said he originally wanted to organize group rides using Citi Bikes, but was unsure whether that would expose him to legal issues. He’s also thinking about how to make Ground Truth more socially interactive as an art project. One possibility is to allow riders to contribute something to the project while they ride. Another would be incorporating additional datasets that could bring different urban or socioeconomic issues into sharper focus. The project could end up evolving significantly in the future. “So it’s really just thinking about what our preconceptions about affordability are,” he said, “and how we can kind of throw a wrench in that at times.” Images by Justin Blinder

articles.summary:
Andy Burnham exchanged messages with somebody posing as White House chief of staff Susie Wiles (whose phone was hacked last year) before becoming suspicious that the contact was an impersonation, Politico reports. The incident has since been reported to the White House, and the undisclosed message contents are reportedly “of no significance.”

articles.title: Trump’s dumb border wall
articles.summary: Border crossings are down. High-tech surveillance is more effective than physical barriers. Still, the Trump administration wants destructive walls anyway.
articles.body: About 22 miles south of the former mining town of Patagonia, Arizona, down a winding, unpaved mountain road that passes cows grazing on open range, stands a cottonwood tree believed to be at least 200 years old. The “grandmother” tree, as some locals call it, is imperiled and already showing signs of stress, almost as if it knows its fate. The leaves are yellowing prematurely, falling to the ground at the height of summer. On July 27th, a construction crew felled three neighboring trees to build an extension of President Donald Trump’s wall along the US-Mexico border. An activist climbed up the last tree standing two days later and ever since, someone has sat on a platform hoisted onto the tree’s branches. They say they’ll sit there as long as it takes, because as long as someone is in the tree, it can’t be cut down. The protest is about more than one cottonwood. “This tree represents a literal line in the sand against border militarization in general,” said Russ McSpadden, the Southwest conservation advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity. In recent weeks, the Department of Homeland Security has revived its effort to wall off the border, dispatching construction crews to remote parts of Texas, Arizona, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation lands to finish Trump’s wall — and has waived environmental laws to get it built, causing backlash from the tiny desert town of Ajo to the even tinier ghost town of Terlingua. This latest construction push is happening despite record-low encounters along the southwestern border. In fact, encounters at the southwest border dropped almost immediately after Trump took office — not because of any new infrastructure, but because he effectively shut down asylum. Despite the steep decline in migrant crossings, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed along party lines in 2025, gave Trump an additional $46.5 billion to finish building the wall.  The border wall is more than just a wall; it’s a vast surveillance network of interconnected drones, towers, and cameras. Even in areas where there’s no visible barrier separating the United States and Mexico, CBP relies on this “virtual wall” to track migrants. This vast surveillance apparatus is far more effective than a wall, and it’s already largely in place. In the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, activists from surrounding communities have set up an encampment on private property near the cottonwood tree to support the protest. They take turns cooking meals and use a pulley system to transport food and water to the person sitting in the tree. They know they’re being watched. Trucks from Vision Quest Solutions, a private security firm that advertises itself as veteran- and Native American-owned, roll up and down the fresh dirt road just south of the tree. The activists track the various contractors that are building the road: Fisher Sand & Gravel, BJ Drilling, Stinger Bridge & Iron, and others. [Image: Homeland Security contractors drive past an ancient cottonwood tree in Lochiel, Arizona. Activists have been occupying the tree since July 29th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/border_wall_tree_sit_e6f222.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Henry, a community organizer from Tucson who is participating in the encampment, said that a DHS helicopter flew “dangerously close” to the tree on August 10th.  “This movement was started and held down for a long time by local environmentalists who care really deeply about these ancient cottonwood trees,” said Henry, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym. He is among a newer group of activists “who see it as an opportunity to physically stop border wall construction.” The planned construction projects differ by region. In Arizona’s San Rafael Valley, where an older fence already divides Mexico and the United States, DHS is building a wall featuring 30-foot-tall steel bollards. Outraged locals, joined by environmentalists from across the country, charge that CBP doesn’t need to build a 30-foot wall to destroy local ecosystems. Over the weekend, contractors started digging into Mariscal Mountain, a massive limestone ridge, ostensibly as part of the survey and design work needed to build its patrol road. Y’all were supposed to tell us about it.” Miller said that he and other locals have been told that the new CBP roads won’t be open to the public; only Border Patrol will be able to use them. “That’s heartbreaking. You’re going to destroy our national park, or take away private landowners’ property, and create roads nobody can use?” he said. According to Mennell, the CBP spokesperson, the National Park Service will decide whether the roads will be open to the public. “You’re taking a wilderness area that’s really hard to get through, really hard to walk through on foot, and now you’re creating a brand-new road? Though Trump received 55.6 percent of the vote in Texas’ Brewster County, the community is almost universally opposed to the wall. Miller has friends and relatives who “voted for Trump without really thinking that he would ever try to build a wall out here,” he said. “And now they are kicking themselves in the ass for voting for him.” Locals share the opinion that the wall isn’t about border security or immigration. Fisher Sand & Gravel, one of the contractors working on the wall in Arizona, reportedly lobbied Trump directly, and was awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract during his first term. On Wednesday, over 100 people attended a protest in Big Bend National Park’s Santa Elena Canyon. Their chants of “no road, no wall, no wire, no way” echoed off the surrounding cliffs. articles.title: Apple squashes EU beef with new App Store rules
articles.summary: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says resolves its disagreements with the European Commission.
articles.body: Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says will resolve its “disagreements with the Commission over business terms and alternative distribution.” As part of the changes, every developer that distributes apps will be moved to a single set of business terms, and digital transactions for apps distributed outside of the App Store will be subject to a Core Technology Commission fee of 5 percent. The new terms go into effect on October 1st. They will include a 26 percent commission for App Store apps that use Apple’s in-app purchase system, or a 20 percent fee for developers using alternate payment providers. Developers must also pay a 15 percent commission on purchases that link out of the app. Apple will reduce these rates for developers in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program. With the new terms, developers can offer both in-app purchases and alternative payment systems in the EU. However, developers must maintain the payment options they choose for 12 months “to provide consistency and clarity for users,” Apple says. There’s also a 5 percent Core Technology Commission on digital transactions in apps distributed on third-party app stores and the web. Apple will no longer charge an initial acquisition fee, store services fee, or the Core Technology Fee, a €0.50 per download fee that applied to apps for each annual install over 1 million.  Web distribution is only available in the EU, Apple says, and the company has eligibility requirements in place for who can actually operate a third-party app marketplace over the web, like being a publicly traded company or having completed a financial audit from a “licensed accountant.” Apple changed its App Store rules last year to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a set of rules regulating Big Tech. The company has remained critical of the regulations and was fined last year after the Commission found that its App Store “anti-steering” practices violated the DMA. Apple lost its bid to exclude the App Store and iOS from the DMA last month. Apple’s updates also include new child safety features for the EU. Kids apps in the App Store can’t have links to websites for finishing transactions, and Apple won’t let App Store apps link out to websites for a purchase if a user is under 13 years old. Users under 18 will have to get permission from a parent or guardian when trying to make a purchase using an alternative payment method inside an App Store app.

articles.title: Meta glasses are a workplace menace
articles.summary: Meta glasses are quickly becoming a problem in workplaces. Public-facing workers are being filmed, harassed, and creeped out by AI-powered smart glasses.
articles.body: In August, Toru Hinkle was stocking shelves at their job at Target when they noticed two customers and asked if they needed any help. The men requested a price check on an item — but even after Hinkle told them the item was $20, the customers asked for the price again and again.  “After a while, I realized that I’m basically being pranked, and I noticed the glasses,” Hinkle says, referring to the frames with a blinking light. They were the Ray-Ban Meta glasses, and the customers were filming. Hinkle eventually called a store manager over, but the pranksters antagonized her, too — asking the price repeatedly, deliberately misgendering Hinkle as “ma’am” and the female manager as “sir.” At one point, Hinkle attempted to stop the recording by saying “Meta, stop recording” out loud, hoping to trigger a voice control setting. The customers pretended to be confused by the accusation that they were recording Hinkle. The confrontation made Hinkle queasy. “I felt like this pit in my stomach just started to build up,” Hinkle recalls. “After this whole exchange happened, the rest of the shift, I was just quiet and didn’t even talk to anyone because I was just so shaken up by it.” Another customer called the police, Hinkle says, and the two men were escorted out of the store. Target declined to comment. The two customers were, in fact, recording Hinkle, and the entire exchange was turned into content for social media. Another Target manager came across the video while scrolling online, without even looking for it. One clip featuring the incident with Hinkle viewed by The Verge had almost 400,000 views on Instagram and 155,000 views on TikTok. Meta has sold millions of pairs of its AI-powered smart glasses over the last several years — but as sales boom, so too has the backlash to the devices. The glasses allow wearers to listen to music or take calls, but the feature that has sparked outrage is the ability to record using them: Many people see them as a new notch in the surveillance apparatus at best, and “pervert” and “creep” glasses at worst.  Ordinarily, if you are recorded against your will, you can try to leave the area or otherwise resist being recorded. But many people are encountering smart glasses for the first time while at their job, especially those who interact with the public, like retail and service workers. In the workplace, smart glasses exacerbate the power imbalance between the customer and the employee, or the boss and subordinate. Resisting invasive technology is risky when you depend on your job to pay rent or buy groceries. It’s harder still when many workplaces don’t yet have policies around a new gadget that the public is grappling with in real time. Service and retail workers in particular have become a target for stealth — and annoying — smart glasses recording. People wearing Meta glasses are going into stores and harassing or “pranking” employees, using the footage for content and making unwitting workers the butt of the joke. The video made of Hinkle and their manager without their consent is the exact kind of content that Instagram has claimed it will now remove — yet the account that uploaded it was filled with similar “prank” videos harassing workers at their jobs.  There’s little recourse for those who have been unknowingly recorded. The worst is when a much taller man stands over her and films her with his Meta glasses. She thinks — hopes — he is not filming down her shirt. But the new method of filming has quickly become part of her daily working environment: On some days, she says up to 10 people an hour will come in wearing smart glasses. The number of routine encounters that are recorded, saved, processed, and accessed later could skyrocket, effectively quantifying even the most mundane or private parts of our lives. Hartzog, the law professor, says, “This is just another way for employees who already have less power in their roles to be further marginalized and dissected, and is part of a larger story about the way in which being an employee means taking on increased suffering as part of the job.”

articles.title: Logitech just got sued for keeping your tariff refund.
articles.summary:
If a company says “we’re charging you more because of Trump’s tariffs” and then gets a full refund from the government, shouldn’t you get a refund? Logitech may join Sony and Nintendo in deciding that in court. In 2025, it raised prices up to 25 percent; so far it’s received $61 million in refunds it doesn’t plan to share.

articles.title: TikTok will pay $400 million to settle DOJ child privacy lawsuit
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice announced on Friday that TikTok will pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit filed in 2024 over allegedly violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA).
articles.body: The US Department of Justice announced on Friday that TikTok will pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit filed in 2024 over allegedly violating the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). In the lawsuit, the DOJ alleged that TikTok collected data from children without notifying parents or obtaining consent and did not delete the accounts when parents requested. TikTok is set to pay $300 million right away and will pay a further $100 million “upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly,” the DOJ says in a press release. The settlement is “one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a COPPA case.” The DOJ also notes that TikTok has “undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices” since the lawsuit was filed and that TikTok has “implemented extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight.” TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. In January, the deal to put TikTok under a new joint ownership structure in the US finally happened.

articles.body:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. stood in the Oval Office last week as President Trump proudly signed an executive order to reduce childhood vaccines, heavily implying a link between vaccines and autism.

But when Kennedy made appearances in California and then hit the campaign trail for Republicans in Iowa over the past week, vaccines weren’t on the agenda at all.

In Iowa, he spoke on the importance of nutrition, youth fitness and the revived presidential fitness test with Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) at a YMCA.

“We think the sedentary condition of many of our children is contributing to this malaise, to the mental health crisis, to the physical fitness crisis, to the chronic disease crisis in our country,” Kennedy said.

Alongside Republican Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, Kennedy announced a new statewide addiction treatment and prevention program. He visited a community health center to participate in a roundtable discussion focused on expanding access to primary and preventive care.

Kennedy even went fishing with Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, who has been endorsed by Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again PAC.

Through all his events over the past week, Kennedy has addressed vaccination — and by extension the country’s measles epidemic — only when asked a direct question.

“We’re doing everything that we can,” Kennedy told reporters in Dubuque, Iowa, about measles, saying the U.S. is in much better shape than other countries.

He blamed the COVID-19 pandemic for a loss of faith in the public health system and declining vaccinations worldwide, without mentioning the new executive order.

“During COVID, people lost faith in the public health system. … My job is to make the public health establishment trustworthy,” Kennedy said.

He is in the middle of a 10-day swing across Iowa, Minnesota and Florida, the White House said , part of his sweeping Make America Healthy Again Tour aimed at keeping MAHA supporters engaged ahead of the midterm elections.

It’s a sign the administration views Kennedy as an important asset in trying to help Republicans keep control of government.

“No administration has done more to address America’s chronic disease epidemic than the Trump administration, from overhauling the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to removing artificial ingredients from our food supply,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement to The Hill.

“Secretary Kennedy and the entire HHS [Health and Human Services] team have been instrumental in these successes, and he will continue touting these historic wins for the American people.”

But Kennedy’s localized messaging highlights the conundrum facing the administration on vaccination and the varied interests of MAHA voters who are not necessarily strong Republican primary midterm voters and don’t necessarily support Trump at all costs.

The MAHA movement, which came about from the political alliance between Kennedy and Trump, is broadly focused on issues like chronic disease and childhood illness. It has elevated issues such as vaccine safety but also corporate interests in federal agencies and the presence of chemical additives and pesticides in the food supply.

“I think that the MAHA agenda has been one of the highest priorities of this administration, and it hasn’t been isolated to one or two issues. It’s really been a pretty big breadth of policy issues that they’ve taken on and had success with,” said David Mansdoerfer, who served in the HHS during the first Trump administration.

Mansdoerfer said he doesn’t think Kennedy is “shying away” from talking about vaccines so much as trying to sell what the administration says are MAHA wins.

“’Whether you agree or disagree with us, we are delivering on the agenda that we promised.’ So, to me, [Kennedy’s appearances are] an opportunity to translate the policy efforts done in D.C. to the local level,” Mansdoerfer said.

The White House and Kennedy had stepped back in recent months from aggressive actions to remake vaccine policy ahead of the midterms, until Trump brought it roaring back to the fore with his executive order aimed at reducing the number of recommended vaccines for the youngest children.

During the Oval Office event, both Kennedy and Trump multiple times hinted at the debunked idea that rising rates of childhood shots have led to an increase in autism diagnoses.

“Genes don’t cause epidemics. You need an environmental toxin,” Kennedy said, while thanking Trump for allowing him to reexamine the childhood immunization schedules.

“Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthier, and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist,” Trump said. “So there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to where it was.”

But 24 hours later, Kennedy arrived in California, where he spent the next three days talking up substance abuse treatment and the administration’s faith-based solutions to addiction and homelessness.

Kennedy also spoke about combatting health fraud — a key priority for the Trump administration.

During a visit to a community health center in the Central Valley, Kennedy was asked about how the vaccine order would impact California.

“The president’s executive order should not change the way that children are vaccinated. In California, the state decides what the vaccination schedule is,” Kennedy said, as first reported by Politico.

articles.title: NAACP slams Navy’s reported talks to swap war hero’s name on carrier with Trump’s
articles.summary: NAACP President Derrick Johnson bashed the Navy Friday following reports that it planned to rename an aircraft carrier — currently named after a Black World War II war hero — and had considered President Trump’s name as a replacement. Johnson wrote in a social media post that the alleged talks surrounding the USS Doris Miller’s…
articles.body:
NAACP President Derrick Johnson bashed the Navy Friday following reports that it planned to rename an aircraft carrier — currently named after a Black World War II war hero — and had considered President Trump’s name as a replacement.

Johnson wrote in a social media post that the alleged talks surrounding the USS Doris Miller’s name are “a slap in the face to every war hero and to every service member who has worn the uniform.”

The aircraft carrier is the first of its kind to carry the name of a Black American, as well as the first named in honor of a sailor’s actions performed while serving in the enlisted ranks. The vessel received the name in 2020 during a ceremony at Pearl Harbor.

Doris Miller served aboard the battleship USS West Virginia when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941. When the attack started, Miller jumped to help wounded sailors before manning an anti-aircraft gun and firing at Japanese planes, despite having no formal training on the weapon.

Before being killed in action in 1943, Miller became the first Black American to receive the Navy Cross for his actions during Pearl Harbor.

“It’s beyond comprehension for a president to want his own name on a Navy ship while our armed forces are living in deteriorating conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln ,” Johnson said.

Though the Navy has not confirmed any reports on the potential renaming of the Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, two unnamed sources told CNN Thursday that there had been conversations within the military branch about changing the vessel’s name to instead honor Trump.

However, the White House has made recent public announcements surrounding alterations to vessels such as the USS Doris Miller, sharing plans in August to replace electromagnetic aircraft launch system catapults — which the Navy credited as being highly effective — with steam-powered catapults .

The White House said the move would “fix critical long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding,” though some experts described the technology as outdated.

Bryan Clark, a senior fellow and director of the Center for Defense Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute, told The Hill that steam catapults are no longer in production , and the Navy bought the last set 20 years ago.

articles.title: Questions rise as US claims deeper control of Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: How much oil is actually getting through the Strait of Hormuz? And is the reward for the Pentagon worth the resources it is expending? Those are some of the key outstanding questions as the Trump administration touts some success in steering tankers through a southern channel of the strait along the coast of Oman. The…
articles.body:
How much oil is actually getting through the Strait of Hormuz ? And is the reward for the Pentagon worth the resources it is expending?

Those are some of the key outstanding questions as the Trump administration touts some success in steering tankers through a southern channel of the strait along the coast of Oman.

The operation has allowed the U.S. to claw back some control from Iran over the passage, which has been largely closed since late February. But these efforts require significant resources from the Pentagon, and the reward is just a fraction of gain in the amount of oil traversing the strait compared to prewar levels.

The administration’s latest measures appear to have at least prevented global oil prices from jumping even higher , though the Brent crude price stood at $94.39 going into this week — up from where it had begun the week prior.

It has not alleviated the pressures Republicans are feeling over the economy and the issue of affordability as the midterm elections in November inch closer.

Petras Katinas, a research fellow in energy and defense with the Royal United Services Institute, said Friday that only three or four vessels have passed through the strait on a daily basis in the month of August — far below the numbers in February, when 35 ships passed inbound and 39 outbound.

U.S. officials, however, told Axios that 40 tankers traversed the waterway Friday night through the southern channel off Oman. They also said the effort had facilitated the transit of about 16 million barrels to the global energy market.

Those figures would represent a major jump in ships transiting the waterway in recent weeks.

Katinas sounded a skeptical tone on the figures.

“I know the White House claims … around 15 to 20 vessels passed the Strait of Hormuz [per day], yet we’ve learned the White House math is not very strong,” he told The Hill.

The United Kingdom’s Navy’s Maritime Trade Operations center also put out a lower estimate, stating that, since Aug. 7, very few vessels have openly transited the strait.

The costs of getting more ships out are expensive, and there are risks to the operation, most notably that it could draw fire from Iran.

“There is a challenge … to the extent that this kind of covert shipping of oil is going on, the extent to which it starts to become more significant, therefore less easy to hide, and perhaps also therefore a more open provocation to Iran,” said Mona Yacoubian, the director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

She suggested the bigger the Pentagon’s operation gets, the more it could attract Iranian attacks.

“We’ve seen the Iranians respond to this kind of a thing already in the past, so it could be that it’s in a bit of a catch-22, where as long as the amounts that are being secreted out are not massive and significant, that type of an operation may be able to continue and … be done without enormous resources,” Yacoubian said.

She added, “But it then doesn’t really have much of an impact on the global markets, which is really the effort here.”

The U.S.-led operation has helped empty tankers enter the Gulf from the Arabian Sea through the strait, pick up oil from countries in the Middle East and then exit, according to Axios .

Such an effort requires significant resources to get a limited amount of oil through the strait. Roughly 20 Navy warships are currently in the Gulf of Oman, including two aircraft carrier strike groups, as well as other military equipment needed to intercept Iranian drones and missiles.

The difficulties those duties carry was reflected in this month’s drama surrounding the USS Abraham Lincoln , which recently returned to port after a lengthy deployment that triggered warnings about mental health crises and poor conditions on the ship.

What the U.S. is moving through the strait is also not enough to cover demand, regardless of the true amount.

“Time depletes global stockpiles further because there’s still a deficit of oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz every day, even with U.S. military power shuttling oil through, and nobody has a good read on how much is going through,” said Rosemary Kelanic, the director of Middle East Engagement at Defense Priorities.

“Maybe it’s 3 million barrels a day, maybe it’s 5 million barrels a day, but it’s not prewar levels. And as long as that’s the case, it’s depleting U.S. and global inventories, and that is decreasing the buffer before prices spike,” she continued.

In an attempt to more quickly bring an end to the conflict, President Trump this week promised an “economic D-Day” and a “crushing” operation to “cripple” Iran as he publicly stepped back from any diplomatic avenues with Tehran.

Those remarks seemed to contribute to oil prices rising at week’s end, as markets feared it signaled a longer war.

On Friday, Trump said the U.S. has no lack of military options in the region, while expressing confidence again in U.S. control of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We’re seeing what happens,” he told reporters ahead of boarding Air Force One en route to South Carolina, adding that the U.S. has “total control of that entire region having to do with the Strait of Hormuz. And that means well into it, the land areas.”

Yacoubian said these public reassurances are a part of the administration’s public relations strategy but don’t necessarily mirror reality.

“To be fair, we aren’t seeing storage tanks run dry yet. We are not at that crisis moment that many have feared,” she said. “Something is at play. What it is exactly and how sustainable it is, I think those have been questions from the start.”

articles.title: State of Texas: Big Bend construction paused, but for how long?
articles.summary: The Trump administration temporarily stopped construction on a controversial border security infrastructure project in Big Bend National Park. The move comes after bipartisan pushback to the plan.
articles.body:
New episodes of State of Texas are on KXAN or the KXAN+ app every Sunday at 8:30 a.m. Don’t want to wait? Scroll down to continue watching this week’s segments now.

AUSTIN (Nexstar) – The Trump administration temporarily stopped construction on a controversial border security infrastructure project in Big Bend National Park. The move comes after bipartisan pushback to the plan.

Earlier this month, images of bulldozers tearing up land and clearing vegetation in the park sparked outrage across the state. Officials with U.S. Customs and Border Protection defended the project, emphasizing that the plan focused on vehicle barriers and road improvements.

The park covers more than 1,252 square miles of land. State Sen. Cesar Blanco (D – El Paso) represents a district that includes large areas of the park. In an interview, he spoke about why the area holds special significance for many Texans.

“Well, it’s one of the most remote places on Earth. It’s beautiful. Lots of wildlife, lots of beautiful plants, landscapes, sunsets,” Blanco explained. “It’s just a place where your cell phone doesn’t work and you can be one with nature.”

“So it’s very important for not just our region, but really for the world,” he added.

After the pause in construction, Blanco traveled to the park to see the aftermath. He posted video on social media showing where construction equipment had cut a path through part of the park.

“This is God’s country. And what’s happening at Big Bend is devastating,” Sen. Blanco wrote in his post. “Once this landscape is destroyed, we can’t simply get it back.”

On Tuesday, Sen. Blanco joined a group that met with Rodney Scott, Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. He said the commissioner was receptive to the concerns Blanco has been hearing from Texans.

“He acknowledged that that CBP moved very quickly and did not do the consultation that should have happened before construction. He apologized. And I think that acknowledgment is important,” Blanco said.

“My message to the commissioner was pretty simple. We can secure the border while protecting the people, the communities, and the natural resources that make Big Bend a special place,” Blanco said of the meeting. The Senator said he highlighted options to use technology as well as placing more agents on foot, on horseback, on ATVs to provide security without damaging natural habitat.

While construction is on hold, it’s not clear how long the pause will last. Blanco says the crucial question is what happens next with the project. He said Scott told him a decision would come in a couple of weeks as to when work would resume. Blanco said it’s not clear what the project will entail moving forward.

“The commissioner was very clear that CBP’s intent is not to build a border wall inside Big Bend National Park, and I appreciate that commitment. But a wall is not the only concern,” Blanco said.

“We still need answers about roads. We need answers about barriers and other construction, including exactly what CBP plans to build and where they’re going to build it,” Blanco added. He noted that construction in the park carries the risk of damage that cannot be undone.

“Once you clear land, carve roads, and permanently alter landscape, you can’t simply put it back the way it was,” Blanco said. “We want to make sure we protect the border, but we also want to make sure that we protect Big Bend. And I believe we can do and that we should do both.”

Coastal Bend crisis leads to calls to strengthen water planning process

Earlier this year, officials in Corpus Christi warned the city was months away from a water emergency . Supply levels had dropped to the point that officials were making hurried plans to implement surcharges and water use reductions that would have impacted roughly 500,000 people and the energy industry in the region.

Flooding rain earlier this summer brought relief, for now. But the way the situation played out is raising questions about the state’s water planning process. A new report from nonprofit Texas 2036 is now calling for changes in the process.

Jeremy Mazur, Director of Infrastructure and Natural Resources Policy at Texas 2036 will discuss the report Monday at a field hearing of the Texas House Natural Resources Committee . He noted that the state’s water planning process was created nearly 30 years ago. Mazur describes it as a “bottom-up process.”

“Regions across the state identify long-term water supply needs, available supplies, and potential water shortages, but also recommend the water supply strategies and projects such as reservoirs and desalination facilities needed to meet those anticipated shortages,” Mazur explained. The regional plans are rolled into the state water plan prepared by the Texas Water Development Board.

The report says the long-term planning process did not project the shortage that pushed Corpus Christi to the verge of a water emergency. Mazur said the data used in the process needs to be reevaluated to reflect current conditions.

“I think one of the big factors is that these plans focus on what’s called the drought of record, which is a historic long-term drought,” Mazur said. He noted that the Coastal Bend region that includes Corpus Christi endured several droughts of record in the decades since the water planning process was created.

“This radically affected the water supply projections within the plans. And so the water supply projections in the earlier plans were projected a lot more water availability than what actually happened to be the case when the drought from this year, which they suspect to be historic and very severe, really decimated the available water supplies in the region,” Mazur said.

The report recommends ways for the Legislature and the Texas Water Development Board to strengthen the planning process, including stress testing for worse droughts and better data verification.

“The lessons learned from our report is not that the plans or the planning process is bad, but it can certainly be perfected with better data and better planning objectives to better identify what we need to do to build the water infrastructure for a drought-prone and growing state,” Mazur said.

Data center growth in Texas fuels AI boom debate

Communities and politicians are starting to push back against an industry fueling both the AI boom and a national debate. While supporters argue the economic benefits more than offset any tax breaks, lawmakers are facing pressure to scale back lucrative incentives ballooning into the billions of dollars.

The Texas Tribune, a reporting partner of KXAN, found 355 operating and 2447 planned data centers across Texas and mapped them in a searchable online database.

“This is the hottest issue in the state right now,” said Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller at a packed town hall in Bastrop on July 22. “Republicans better wake up because the Democrats are right on this issue, and they’re owning it.”

Miller, a Republican, has called for a one-year moratorium on data centers arguing lawmakers need to establish better guardrails and oversight.

Gov. Greg Abbott has directed Texas energy regulators to conduct a comprehensive audit of data center projects seeking to connect to the state’s power grid, saying no project should move forward until officials determine whether the developments comply with state requirements.

“Our top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life,” Abbott said in a statement. “Any project that fails to comply with the requirements set forth by the PUCT and ERCOT, and by state law, must be denied connection to the Texas grid. Simply put, Texans must come first.”

According to the governor’s office, ERCOT is currently considering more than 474 gigawatts of requests to connect to the Texas electric grid. State officials said about 90% of those requests come from data center projects.

Texas landowners urge governor to call special session on transmission lines

Dozens of landowners from across Texas gathered at the Capitol Wednesday, urging Gov. Greg Abbott to call a special legislative session aimed at stopping proposed 765-kilovolt transmission lines that would cross private property throughout the state.

The rally coincided with a Texas House Committee on State Affairs hearing examining data centers and 765-kV transmission lines, where opponents of the projects planned to provide public testimony.

The transmission line projects have faced months of opposition from landowners and advocacy groups.

Texas senators and Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick recently called on the Public Utility Commission of Texas to delay action on certain transmission line applications while lawmakers review the issue further.

Wearing yellow bandanas, landowners gathered outside the Capitol Wednesday morning.

“To the legislators inside all of these buildings, do not mistake ordinary people for powerless people,” said Mia Sarot with the Hill Country Land and Legacy Alliance at the rally.

Another speaker called for immediate action.

“We are here today not to beg, but to demand a special session,” said Sheila Hemphill, president of Texas Right to Know.

Supporters said they hope a special session would stop construction of proposed 765-kV transmission lines and give lawmakers another opportunity to review the projects.
