AUSTIN (Nexstar) – The Trump administration temporarily stopped construction on a controversial border security infrastructure project in Big Bend National Park. The move comes after bipartisan pushback to the plan.

Earlier this month, images of bulldozers tearing up land and clearing vegetation in the park sparked outrage across the state. Officials with U.S. Customs and Border Protection defended the project, emphasizing that the plan focused on vehicle barriers and road improvements.

The park covers more than 1,252 square miles of land. State Sen. Cesar Blanco (D – El Paso) represents a district that includes large areas of the park. In an interview, he spoke about why the area holds special significance for many Texans.

“Well, it’s one of the most remote places on Earth. It’s beautiful. Lots of wildlife, lots of beautiful plants, landscapes, sunsets,” Blanco explained. “It’s just a place where your cell phone doesn’t work and you can be one with nature.”
“So it’s very important for not just our region, but really for the world,” he added.
After the pause in construction, Blanco traveled to the park to see the aftermath. He posted video on social media showing where construction equipment had cut a path through part of the park.
“This is God’s country. And what’s happening at Big Bend is devastating,” Sen. Blanco wrote in his post. “Once this landscape is destroyed, we can’t simply get it back.”

On Tuesday, Sen. Blanco joined a group that met with Rodney Scott, Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. He said the commissioner was receptive to the concerns Blanco has been hearing from Texans.

“He acknowledged that that CBP moved very quickly and did not do the consultation that should have happened before construction. He apologized. And I think that acknowledgment is important,” Blanco said.

“My message to the commissioner was pretty simple. We can secure the border while protecting the people, the communities, and the natural resources that make Big Bend a special place,” Blanco said of the meeting. The Senator said he highlighted options to use technology as well as placing more agents on foot, on horseback, on ATVs to provide security without damaging natural habitat.

While construction is on hold, it’s not clear how long the pause will last. Blanco says the crucial question is what happens next with the project. He said Scott told him a decision would come in a couple of weeks as to when work would resume. Blanco said it’s not clear what the project will entail moving forward.
“The commissioner was very clear that CBP’s intent is not to build a border wall inside Big Bend National Park, and I appreciate that commitment. But a wall is not the only concern,” Blanco said.

“We still need answers about roads. We need answers about barriers and other construction, including exactly what CBP plans to build and where they’re going to build it,” Blanco added. He noted that construction in the park carries the risk of damage that cannot be undone.

“Once you clear land, carve roads, and permanently alter landscape, you can’t simply put it back the way it was,” Blanco said. “We want to make sure we protect the border, but we also want to make sure that we protect Big Bend. And I believe we can do and that we should do both.”
Coastal Bend crisis leads to calls to strengthen water planning process

Earlier this year, officials in Corpus Christi warned the city was months away from a water emergency . Supply levels had dropped to the point that officials were making hurried plans to implement surcharges and water use reductions that would have impacted roughly 500,000 people and the energy industry in the region.

Flooding rain earlier this summer brought relief, for now. But the way the situation played out is raising questions about the state’s water planning process. A new report from nonprofit Texas 2036 is now calling for changes in the process.

Jeremy Mazur, Director of Infrastructure and Natural Resources Policy at Texas 2036 will discuss the report Monday at a field hearing of the Texas House Natural Resources Committee . He noted that the state’s water planning process was created nearly 30 years ago. Mazur describes it as a “bottom-up process.”

“Regions across the state identify long-term water supply needs, available supplies, and potential water shortages, but also recommend the water supply strategies and projects such as reservoirs and desalination facilities needed to meet those anticipated shortages,” Mazur explained. The regional plans are rolled into the state water plan prepared by the Texas Water Development Board.

The report says the long-term planning process did not project the shortage that pushed Corpus Christi to the verge of a water emergency. Mazur said the data used in the process needs to be reevaluated to reflect current conditions.

“I think one of the big factors is that these plans focus on what’s called the drought of record, which is a historic long-term drought,” Mazur said. He noted that the Coastal Bend region that includes Corpus Christi endured several droughts of record in the decades since the water planning process was created.

“This radically affected the water supply projections within the plans. And so the water supply projections in the earlier plans were projected a lot more water availability than what actually happened to be the case when the drought from this year, which they suspect to be historic and very severe, really decimated the available water supplies in the region,” Mazur said.
The report recommends ways for the Legislature and the Texas Water Development Board to strengthen the planning process, including stress testing for worse droughts and better data verification.

“The lessons learned from our report is not that the plans or the planning process is bad, but it can certainly be perfected with better data and better planning objectives to better identify what we need to do to build the water infrastructure for a drought-prone and growing state,” Mazur said.
Data center growth in Texas fuels AI boom debate

Communities and politicians are starting to push back against an industry fueling both the AI boom and a national debate. While supporters argue the economic benefits more than offset any tax breaks, lawmakers are facing pressure to scale back lucrative incentives ballooning into the billions of dollars.
The Texas Tribune, a reporting partner of KXAN, found 355 operating and 2447 planned data centers across Texas and mapped them in a searchable online database.

“This is the hottest issue in the state right now,” said Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller at a packed town hall in Bastrop on July 22. “Republicans better wake up because the Democrats are right on this issue, and they’re owning it.”
Miller, a Republican, has called for a one-year moratorium on data centers arguing lawmakers need to establish better guardrails and oversight.

Gov. Greg Abbott has directed Texas energy regulators to conduct a comprehensive audit of data center projects seeking to connect to the state’s power grid, saying no project should move forward until officials determine whether the developments comply with state requirements.

According to the governor’s office, ERCOT is currently considering more than 474 gigawatts of requests to connect to the Texas electric grid. State officials said about 90% of those requests come from data center projects.

articles.title: Oz: MMR vaccine ‘is not a lethal vaccine’
articles.summary: Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), noted Sunday the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is not lethal, contradicting President Trump. “The MMR vaccine is not a lethal vaccine, and it is offered in other countries,” Oz told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”…
articles.body:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), noted Sunday the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is not lethal, contradicting President Trump.

“The MMR vaccine is not a lethal vaccine, and it is offered in other countries,” Oz told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation .”

After signing an executive order to alter federal guidance on the childhood vaccination schedule, Trump claimed the MMR vaccine was “lethal” in some cases.

The president’s order recommended that physicians split up the combined MMR shot, which has been available since 1971. Doctors recommend that children receive the vaccine at 12 to 15 months and again at 4 to 6 years.

“Together there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” the president said in the Oval Office, referring to the MMR vaccine. “And separately it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.”

In addition to splitting up the MMR shot, Trump’s order recommends that all children receive just 11 core vaccinations. Children at a high risk of infection should receive more vaccines, while others can still access vaccines after consulting with a doctor.

Oz said Sunday the order, which multiple medical experts have criticized , is intended to ensure Americans have “a choice” in deciding whether to vaccinate their children.

“The request of the president is to make sure that states offer parents either eligibility because of religious beliefs or other reasons why they may not want to have their kids take all the vaccines in order,” the CMS administrator told Brennan.

articles.title: Zeldin warns against banning data centers in US, citing China
articles.summary: Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), on Sunday warned against banning data centers, citing implications for the U.S. in the artificial intelligence race to outpace China. “There’s been a push from some states where they’re talking about a statewide moratorium and what I’ve found is that most of this country wants to make…
articles.body:
Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), on Sunday warned against banning data centers, citing implications for the U.S. in the artificial intelligence race to outpace China.

“There’s been a push from some states where they’re talking about a statewide moratorium and what I’ve found is that most of this country wants to make sure the United States wins this race to be the AI capital of the world, that we do not relinquish this to China,” Zeldin said during a Sunday appearance on John Catsimatidis’s radio show “The Cats Roundtable” on 77 WABC.

“At the same time, they have important questions about how data centers get built,” he added.

Residents nationwide have raised concerns with the increase in energy costs and environmental impacts due to the development of data centers near their neighborhoods.

A Fox News poll released in late July found that 70 percent of voters oppose the building of a data center in their area to support AI, with 78 percent in support of slowing construction to address environmental and community concerns.

It’s been a major topic for candidates in midterms as President Trump aims to encourage more data centers while urging corporate companies to mitigate the increased costs through his ratepayer protection pledge.

So far, Meta, Amazon, Google and 100 others have agreed to pay for increased energy costs under the Trump administration’s voluntary pledge.

“We have to make sure that these projects are a net provider onto the grid, not a net taker. And we have to make sure that they are making important reuse 100 percent recyclable water … or better if they don’t need water at all. They need to be responsible users of water,” Zeldin said.

“But what we can’t do is just say, well, let’s not have any data centers built all across the entire country and let’s just let China win,” he added.

The EPA administrator urged people to “realize” how much daily life relies “right now on data centers.”

“So let’s ask the questions, let’s be responsible, let’s do it right. But let’s make sure that we win this race in the United States,” he added.

articles.title: In 1981, N. R. Narayana Murthy borrowed â¹10,000 from wife, Sudha Murty, to start Infosys; Decades later, it became an IT giant: A story of their unshakable bond
articles.summary: Relationships News: N. R. Narayana Murthy and Sudha Murty first met in Pune in the mid-1970s through a mutual friend. Books became one of their early connections. Murthy .
articles.body: N. R. Narayana Murthy and Sudha Murty first met in Pune in the mid-1970s through a mutual friend. Books became one of their early connections. Murthy later joked that he tried to impress her with his collection, while she was more interested in the books than in him.Their relationship grew before either had become a household name. Murthy was an idealistic young engineer with ambitions of becoming an entrepreneur. Sudha was building her own career and had already established herself as an engineer.That difference mattered. Their marriage was never simply the story of one person chasing a dream while the other stood quietly behind.The â¹10,000 decisionIn 1981, Murthy wanted to start a software company. But there was one immediate problem: money.Infosys' own records confirm that the company was incorporated in 1981 with paid-in capital of â¹10,000, reportedly borrowed from Sudha.Sudha later recalled having â¹10,250 in savings. She kept â¹250 and gave the remaining â¹10,000 to Murthy. Her caution had a reason. His earlier venture, Softronics, had failed within a year.She also gave him three years to make the new venture work before finding a proper job again. It was not blind faith. It was a calculated risk taken by someone who understood exactly what could go wrong.She funded Infosys, but was not a founderOne of the more complicated parts of their story came after the money was given.Sudha was not included in the Infosys founding team. Murthy later explained that he did not want to build the company as a family-run organisation, even though he acknowledged that she was highly qualified.That decision hurt her for a couple of years. Yet time changed how she viewed it. Sudha later said she was glad she did not become part of Infosys because her work through the Infosys Foundation allowed her to touch many lives.This is where their relationship becomes more interesting than the familiar â¹10,000 anecdote. They did not always agree. They also did not have to build the same career to remain partners.From struggle to a global companyThe early Infosys years demanded sacrifice from the entire family. Sudha has described building a company as something that requires support and sacrifice from the family.The gamble eventually transformed into something far bigger. Infosys, started in Pune by seven engineers, later became India's first IT company to be listed on Nasdaq in 1999.Murthy has recalled sitting under the bright lights at Nasdaq as one of his proudest professional moments. The â¹10,000 that once represented uncertainty had become part of a much larger story.Decades later, respect remains the strongest threadPerhaps the most revealing part of their relationship is how they speak about each other now.Sudha, meanwhile, has spoken more plainly about marriage. âWhen you are married, you are bound to fight,â she said, adding that disagreements are part of being husband and wife.That may be the most relatable part of their story. Their bond was not built on never arguing or always agreeing. It survived because both built independent identities while continuing to respect the person beside them.The â¹10,000 was important. But the bigger investment was trust, even when the future was uncertain.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly reported accounts and statements by Sudha Murty, N. R. Narayana Murthy and Infosys.

articles.title: Back-to-school season expected to worsen record measles outbreak
articles.summary: With kids returning to school amid the worst year of measles in more than 30 years and as a record number of children report exemptions from vaccines, the likelihood that the spread of measles will worsen is all but certain according to public health leaders. The majority of U.S. public schools will have begun their…
articles.body:
With kids returning to school amid the worst year of measles in more than 30 years and as a record number of children report exemptions from vaccines, the likelihood that the spread of measles will worsen is all but certain according to public health leaders.

The majority of U.S. public schools will have begun their 2026-27 academic years by the end of August, and students will be returning as the country has recorded nearly 3,000 measles cases across 47 jurisdictions and 36 new outbreaks this year.

The number of measles cases this year has marked the worst seen in the country in 35 years, with last year already having been one of the poorest in recent history. Public health experts are anticipating the return to school will worsen the current spread of the disease.

“Because of the situation that we are finding ourselves in, we can definitely anticipate seeing more of what we’ve seen all year long,” Lori Freeman, CEO of the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO), told The Hill. “There’s nothing that I can think of that’s going to stem the tide of what we’ve experienced; the only thing that’s going to turn it back is by addressing people’s fears about immunization, vaccination, and getting people vaccinated.”

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, directed blame toward the Trump administration for politicizing vaccines.

“The worst part about this two-year surge in measles is that it was completely avoidable,” Weingarten said in a statement to The Hill. “Instead of trusting pediatricians, the science and the data, this administration turned vaccine hesitancy into a culture war, peddled disinformation, and undermined and underfunded the CDC which now struggles to prevent outbreaks of a disease that was nearly eradicated.”

“This leaves schools, hospitals — and the students and patients they serve — vulnerable and exposed, with educators and healthcare workers serving as first responders to waves of infections that never should have spread in the first place,” she added.

And as measles cases continue to rise, new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released this week found that nonmedical vaccine exemptions among kindergartners reached an all-time high during the 2025-26 school year — at 4.2 percent.

Among states reporting increases, 24 reported exemptions exceeding 5 percent.

Kindergartner measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination rates last school year were found to be 92.4 percent, still less than the 95 percent coverage rate considered ideal for preventing widespread outbreaks. The vaccination rate has been on a steady decline since the 2019-20 school year, the last time the country had a coverage rate of about 95 percent.

In a briefing on staying healthy during the back-to-school season, experts with the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) emphasized the particular importance of keeping up to date on immunizations this school year.

“A single unvaccinated child in a school full of unvaccinated classmates can start an outbreak that spreads to dozens of families within days,” Dr. Julia Rosebush, associate professor in the department of pediatrics at the University of Chicago, said in the briefing.

Experts like Freeman said tracking which students are unvaccinated can be tricky as it can step on parental rights. She noted that school nurses often have this information and advised that they develop updated emergency operations plans for when measles transmissions occur in classrooms.

Measles is one of the most virulent infectious diseases, with one infected individual capable of infecting nine out of 10 unvaccinated people they’re exposed to.

Further complicating matters is the Trump administration’s push to rewrite long-held vaccine policy.

Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split up by disease, which would in effect separate two vaccine appointments into six. Since he signed the order, one state after another has affirmed plans to keep the preexisting vaccine guidance, including California, New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania.

Acting on Trump’s executive order is also currently unfeasible as no manufacturers in the U.S. make monovalent vaccines individually targeting measles, mumps or rubella.

Freeman said her organization is focused on identifying likely pockets of unvaccinated communities that could harbor measles infections that spread to others.

“We know these susceptible pockets are geographically in neighborhoods, sometimes concentrated in social networks and religious communities,” said Freeman.

While organizations like the IDSA are supporting vaccination efforts, Freeman said NACCHO is taking a different approach.

Because of how fraught the conversation around vaccinations has become, Freeman’s group is focusing on listening and educational sessions as a starting point, targeting communities and partnering with trusted leaders to open up discussions about immunization.

“We cannot continue to kind of force vaccinations down the throats of people who are hesitant. We have to start in a different place, and that place really is listening and hearing and understanding what their questions are first,” she said.

Kindergartner measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination rates last school year were found to be 92.4 percent, still less than the 95 percent coverage rate considered ideal for preventing widespread outbreaks. The vaccination rate has been on a steady decline since the 2019-20 school year, the last time the country had a coverage rate of about 95 percent.

In a briefing on staying healthy during the back-to-school season, experts with the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) emphasized the particular importance of keeping up to date on immunizations this school year.

“A single unvaccinated child in a school full of unvaccinated classmates can start an outbreak that spreads to dozens of families within days,” Dr. Julia Rosebush, associate professor in the department of pediatrics at the University of Chicago, said in the briefing.

Experts like Freeman said tracking which students are unvaccinated can be tricky as it can step on parental rights. She noted that school nurses often have this information and advised that they develop updated emergency operations plans for when measles transmissions occur in classrooms.
Measles is one of the most virulent infectious diseases, with one infected individual capable of infecting nine out of 10 unvaccinated people they’re exposed to.
Further complicating matters is the Trump administration’s push to rewrite long-held vaccine policy.

Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be split up by disease, which would in effect separate two vaccine appointments into six. Since he signed the order, one state after another has affirmed plans to keep the preexisting vaccine guidance, including California, New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania.
Acting on Trump’s executive order is also currently unfeasible as no manufacturers in the U.S. make monovalent vaccines individually targeting measles, mumps or rubella.
Freeman said her organization is focused on identifying likely pockets of unvaccinated communities that could harbor measles infections that spread to others.
“We know these susceptible pockets are geographically in neighborhoods, sometimes concentrated in social networks and religious communities,” said Freeman.
While organizations like the IDSA are supporting vaccination efforts, Freeman said NACCHO is taking a different approach.

Because of how fraught the conversation around vaccinations has become, Freeman’s group is focusing on listening and educational sessions as a starting point, targeting communities and partnering with trusted leaders to open up discussions about immunization.

“We cannot continue to kind of force vaccinations down the throats of people who are hesitant. We have to start in a different place, and that place really is listening and hearing and understanding what their questions are first,” she said.

articles.title: Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from WNBA game after confrontation with player
articles.summary: Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected Sunday from a WNBA game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky after a verbal altercation with Chicago’s Natasha Cloud. Late in the third quarter, Cloud approached Freedom, who was sitting courtside and wearing a shirt that read, “Woman: noun. Adult human female.” Video shows the Sky…
articles.body:
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected Sunday from a WNBA game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky after a verbal altercation with Chicago’s Natasha Cloud.

Late in the third quarter, Cloud approached Freedom, who was sitting courtside and wearing a shirt that read, “Woman: noun. Adult human female.” Video shows the Sky guard pointing and yelling at the former NBA player, who was standing up with his arms stretched out and shouting back.

A security guard then escorted Freedom out of the arena. The Fever went on to win the game, 113-90, to move to 25-14 on the season.

Freedom, who last played for the Boston Celtics in the 2021-22 season, declared for the 2027 WNBA draft earlier this month.

Under WNBA policy, only women are eligible to play. A transgender woman has not competed in the league, according to ESPN, and the WNBA does not have a specific policy on the matter.

Before the game, Freedom posted on the social platform X a photo of a woman giving him the middle finger outside of Wintrust Arena in Chicago.

“Careful what you wish for, @WNBA,” Freedom later wrote on X , sharing a photo of him sitting courtside in his shirt. “Freedom of speech never looked this good. Somehow controversial.”

The former NBA player told Fox News that Cloud approached him after he celebrated Fever wing Sophie Cunningham making a 3-pointer.

“I put my hands up to celebrate. … Natasha came back and started screaming and yelling and said, ‘[Cunningham is] not going to sleep with you,’” Freedom, who joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game, said.

For a profile of her published by ESPN in July, Cunningham said, “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

But Cunningham also said she does not hate transgender people and is “very much in the middle” politically.

articles.title: Ford and Stellantis Drop 4% as Trump Sets 50% Auto Tariffs on Canada, General Motors Slips
articles.summary: A Truth Social post landed at the open and immediately sent Detroit's Big Three into a tailspin, but the selloff is hitting Ford and Stellantis twice as hard...
articles.body:
Ford (F) and Stellantis (STLA) each fell 4% after Trump announced 50% tariffs on all Canadian vehicles and parts starting January 2027.

Canada's ambassador Mark Wiseman said the written trade text diverged from what Canada believed it agreed to, collapsing U.S.-Canada talks.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Stellantis didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today .

Ford ( NYSE:F ) stock is down 4% to $13.87 in Monday mid-morning trading after President Trump announced a sharp escalation in auto tariffs targeting Canadian imports. Meanwhile, Stellantis ( NYSE:STLA ) shares are also down 4% to $5.19, while General Motors ( NYSE:GM ) stock is down 2% to $86.28.

The selling is sorting within Detroit's Big Three, with Ford and Stellantis taking the harder hit on the tape today. For context, the Global X Autonomous & Electric Vehicles ETF ( NASDAQ:DRIV ) is down 2% to $34.25.

The tariff itself isn't yet in force, and Trump's announced 50% duty on Canadian vehicles and parts is set to take effect January 1, 2027, so Monday's tape is repricing an announced future cost. Ford stock was up 17% year to date through Friday's close, so today's slide erodes a slice of that lead. Stellantis has traded well below year-end levels heading in, which magnifies the sting for shareholders already sitting on losses.

Truth Social Post Triggers the Auto Selloff

In a Truth Social post Monday, Trump wrote, "On January first, 2027, tariffs on all cars, trucks, both large and small, automotive parts, and steel, will be increased to 50%." He accused Canada of "ripping off" the United States and cited a $60 billion trade deficit as justification for the escalation. The post landed at the open of the week and immediately pressured cross-border auto exposure across the Detroit names.

The auto action follows the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade talks late Friday. Separately, Washington applied 50% tariffs to about $20 billion of Canadian goods after talks broke down, 5% of Canada's exports to the U.S., covering electronics, industrial machinery, dairy, paper goods, appliances, and agricultural equipment. That levy is distinct from the forward-dated auto duty, and Canada announced counter-tariffs scheduled to take effect September 8.

Why Talks Collapsed and Where Automakers Fit

Canada's ambassador to the U.S., Mark Wiseman, told Bloomberg that Canada "needed medium and heavy duty vehicles to be included" in any tariff relief, noting the issue directly affects General Motors and Ford, both of which operate assembly in Canada. He stated, "That's just something we could not accept because we want to protect the existence of an automotive assembly industry in Canada for cars, light trucks, you know, medium trucks and heavy-duty trucks."

articles.title: Scott Bessent’s $1 Trillion Bond Market Fight — Treasury Yields Aren’t Buying It
articles.summary: Scott Bessent is sitting on nearly $1 trillion and signaling he will use it to wrestle long-term Treasury yields back down, but the bond market keeps shruggi...
articles.body:
Bessent doubled Treasury buybacks to $4 billion per operation, but the 30-year yield rebounded to 5.247% within 24 hours, erasing all gains.

The TGA's $1 trillion sounds powerful, but usable funds are only somewhere between $100 billion and $200 billion, barely enough to shift the weighted-average maturity of federal debt.

Treasury wants lower long-term yields while the Fed battles inflation, a direct policy collision that could punish the dollar if private investors don't return.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now .

The bond market has become the place where Washington's promises meet hard financial reality. Long-term Treasury yields have climbed as investors demand compensation for inflation, deficits, geopolitical risk, and an enormous supply of government debt.

That makes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's latest maneuver important for investors well beyond the bond market. Treasury is trying to put a floor under prices at the long end, but the market is making clear that liquidity support is not the same thing as fixing the underlying fiscal math.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Treasury announced that it would at least double the maximum size of its liquidity-support buybacks for 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year nominal Treasuries from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation. The change begins Sept. 9 and runs through the Nov. 4 quarterly refunding. Treasury says these purchases target older, less-liquid "off-the-run" securities to improve market functioning — not reduce overall federal debt.

The market initially listened. The 30-year yield dropped nearly 10 basis points on Aug. 19 to 5.187%, after reaching 5.337% the previous day, its highest level since 2007. The 10-year yield fell to 4.651%.

Then reality arrived. President Donald Trump warned of an "economic D-Day" against Iran, while oil remained above $90 a barrel. On Aug. 20, the 10-year yield climbed 4.7 basis points to 4.70%, while the 30-year reached 5.247%. Treasury's one-day victory had largely evaporated.

Washington is flooding the market with billions to suppress interest rates, yet yields are still hitting decade highs. It's a high-stakes collision between government intervention and fiscal truth. © 24/7 Wall St.

Bessent subsequently suggested the $4 billion figure could be exceeded. On Aug. 24, Treasury officials indicated the department is considering using its Treasury General Account (TGA), which was approaching $1 trillion, to fund expanded buybacks.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s Social Security reset is coming even after DOGE’s death — protect your check whether you like him or not
articles.summary: DOGE gutted staffing and pushed Social Security toward a tech-driven future. Now retirees must prepare for an agency with fewer workers and a looming funding...
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Elon Musk may have left Washington, and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) may be dead, but the changes the agency helped unleash on Social Security are very much alive.

DOGE officially reached its planned expiration date (1) on July 4, 2026, after shutting down months earlier. The initiative launched sweeping efforts to shrink the federal workforce and overhaul government agencies, with more than 260,000 federal employees leaving government service in 2025 amid layoffs, early retirements, deferred resignations and a hiring freeze.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

JPMorgan sees gold hitting $5,000/oz by Q4 — and savvy investors are protecting their wealth with a tax-advantaged Gold IRA. Get your free guide from Priority Gold

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Social Security offers one of the clearest examples of what DOGE left behind.

Nearly 8,000 employees have left (2) the agency since President Donald Trump returned to office, according to Office of Personnel Management data cited by the Federal News Network. The Social Security Administration (SSA) entered 2026 with roughly 50,000 employees, leaving the agency with its smallest workforce in decades, even as it serves around 75 million beneficiaries. Musk himself has since called DOGE only "somewhat successful" and said he wouldn't undertake the effort again.

Yet, Social Security is still moving ahead with an increasingly technology-driven future. Its newly released strategic plan (3) for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 describes its goals as "transformative," with a focus on faster, more reliable service, technology and productivity. That approach builds on changes DOGE pushed at the agency under Musk (4), including workforce reductions, greater reliance on online services and an explicit effort to use technology and automation to improve efficiency.

Can technology make up for thousands of lost workers?

The American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), which represents SSA workers, says the agency has long been understaffed and under-resourced. The union is calling for Congress to provide roughly $3 billion in additional funding and eventually add 20,000 employees.

The SSA says (5) its modernization push is working. The agency reported that wait times at field offices fell 23% in fiscal 2025 compared with 2024, while its initial disability claims backlog fell 25%.

articles.title: Robotaxis are real now — so is the pushback
articles.summary: Robotaxi companies like Waymo and Zoox are running into obstacles in an increasing number of cities as the fight to shape the rules over driverless operations intensifies.
articles.body: Robotaxis are expanding. So is the fight over the rules governing them. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul withdrew a proposal earlier this year that would have opened the door to driverless robotaxis outside New York City after taxi drivers, unions, and state lawmakers opposed it. Six months later, commercial driverless service remains illegal in the state, and legalization efforts are stalled. In DC, labor unions are fighting legislation that would legalize commercial robotaxis, while lawmakers are weighing a 200-vehicle cap and a 15-cent-per-mile fee that would fund Metro upgrades and aid workers displaced by autonomous vehicles. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours. In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws. And while Congress has yet to pass comprehensive robotaxi legislation, federal regulators have stepped up their scrutiny. The Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration recently warned autonomous-vehicle companies that vehicles unable to safely interact with police, firefighters, and other first responders pose a danger to the public. Even in states that have broadly welcomed autonomous vehicles, governments are grappling with how to oversee them. Texas this year began enforcing new permitting requirements for commercial AV operators, while cities in Florida have complained that state preemption laws leave them with little power to respond to problems on their own streets. Taxi drivers, labor unions, and safety advocates have fought autonomous vehicles for years. What’s changing is the scale and immediacy of the fight. Now that robotaxis have burst free from the pages of science fiction and onto actual city streets, policymakers are confronting a messier reality filled with questions about safety, regulation, growth, and jobs. They’re having to decide how quickly fleets should be allowed to expand, what companies must prove before they do, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. Waymo, the market leader, is currently operating more than 3,500 vehicles publicly in 11 US cities. Zoox — a purpose-built robotaxi without a steering wheel that bears a striking resemblance to a toaster — just began offering paid rides in Las Vegas and continues to offer free trips to users of its Explorer program in San Francisco as it collects feedback. It’s testing in a total of 10 cities and plans to extend the Explorer program to Austin and Miami later this year. Tesla, which began its Robotaxi rollout with a safety monitor aboard more than a year ago, appears to finally be growing its unsupervised fleet ahead of launching its purpose-built robotaxi, the Cybercab, later this month. Still, for all the political attention, robotaxis remain a tiny share of the US ridehailing market. While Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides a week, Uber handles about 40 million trips a day globally. At that scale, robotaxis haven’t yet displaced many driving jobs or fundamentally changed how cities move. But their visibility vastly exceeds their market share, especially when a driverless car stops in the wrong place during a blackout or interferes with an emergency response. And the consequences could look very different as autonomous fleets grow from thousands of vehicles to hundreds of thousands. That’s why the battles taking shape across the country are increasingly about the terms of expansion: what companies have to prove before they grow, what they owe cities and workers, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gettyimages-2286668940.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] What the critics want In many places, the robotaxi rollout has outpaced the rules governing it. “Robotaxis are popping up all over the place,” said Shua Sanchez, national campaign director of SAVE-US, a nonprofit advocating for stricter state AV legislation in the absence of federal rules. “The state legislatures don’t have experience with this technology, and there aren’t good laws on the books to regulate them.” SAVE-US is working with lawmakers in New Jersey and New York on a three-pronged approach. It wants multi-stage testing and commercial-deployment permits, under which companies would have to demonstrate their vehicles can operate safely with a small fleet before adding more cars, while continuing to share safety data after commercial service begins. It also wants autonomous vehicles to use multiple kinds of sensors, rather than relying on cameras alone (as Tesla does), and is calling for restrictions on marketing terms like “Autopilot” or “Full Self-Driving” for consumer driver-assist features when the systems still require human oversight. The group isn’t opposed to autonomous vehicles, Sanchez said, but is “pro the safe development of technology.” He added that AV safety isn’t a settled question, and that even a strong record today doesn’t guarantee the same after a software or hardware change. Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), who has pushed for greater federal oversight of AVs, makes a similar argument about transparency. “Autonomous vehicle companies are making huge claims about how their technology is going to save lives,” Markey told The Verge in a statement. “But right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.” Markey has investigated AV companies’ use of remote human operators and introduced legislation that would require them to regularly report safety data. "“Right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.”" - Sen. Ed Markey “Communities deserve transparency and consistent oversight before we let Big Tech invade their public roads,” he said. But safety is only part of the fight. For labor groups, the stakes are also economic. Peter Finn, Teamsters international vice president at large, called autonomous vehicles an “existential threat” to the work his members do. He pointed to the enormous number of jobs potentially affected by autonomous driving beyond rideshare drivers, including truckers, delivery drivers, and other commercial drivers. Like other groups in the robotaxi debate, the Teamsters insist they aren’t opposed to new technology in principle. But that still leaves them staking out positions that would sharply constrain how autonomous vehicles are deployed.  That includes requiring heavy-duty autonomous vehicles like semitrucks to have a trained human operator aboard — legislation the Teamsters have twice pushed in California, only to see Gov. Gavin Newsom veto it. Finn said the Teamsters plan to pursue the issue again. “If the technology is solely designed to automate and eliminate labor costs, the only entity benefiting from that is corporations,” Finn said. The Teamsters’ immediate legislative priority isn’t robotaxis themselves so much as what it sees coming next. To Finn, Waymo and Zoox are precursors to a much larger fight over autonomous driving. He pointed specifically to Zoox’s ownership by Amazon, arguing that similar technology could eventually be applied to package delivery. Zoox and Waymo both said their current focus remains their robotaxi services. Taken together, the objections go beyond any one safety rule or labor concern. AV resistance has become part of a broader backlash to Big Tech’s growing physical footprint, from data centers to Flock cameras. Companies are pouring enormous sums into new infrastructure, and many residents are still asking what, exactly, they get in return for having it in their communities. [Image: Tesla Cybercabs are lined up on a lot at Tesla Giga Texas in Austin, Wednesday, April 8th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gettyimages-2270749488.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Even robotaxi companies want rules Robotaxi companies, meanwhile, are trying to get ahead of the backlash — and sidestep a patchwork of confusing state and local laws — by helping shape the rules themselves. That includes supporting certain regulations while pushing back on others they see as too restrictive. “I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated,” Zoox CEO Aicha Evans recently said on Fox Business in response to NHTSA’s warnings about unsafe interactions with emergency vehicles. Zoox said it is also trying to head off conflicts before entering new markets. Ron Thaniel, the company’s senior director of policy and regulatory affairs, said Zoox establishes lines of communication with local and state officials and conducts hands-on engagement with first responders before launching in a city. As the industry expands, he said, Zoox sees “an opportunity at the federal level to more uniformly regulate autonomous vehicles.” Waymo told The Verge much the same thing. “I think there definitely needs to be some regulation,” Waymo global head of public policy Justin Kintz said. “They’re powered by incredible technology that makes the world a safer place, but it still needs oversight from the federal government, from states, and from cities in the same way that they manage human drivers today.” "“I want to unequivocally say we agree with the administrator and the administration and the regulatory agency. We need to be regulated.”" - Zoox CEO Aicha Evans Zoox and Waymo are hardly alone in wanting clearer rules. The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association, which counts both companies as members, has said only about half of US states have passed laws that allow vehicles to operate without humans. The industry group believes states should establish a legal framework for AVs, require first-responder interaction plans, and set minimum requirements before vehicles can operate without a human driver. (The association didn’t respond to requests for more specifics.) Waymo said it has long advocated for a national AV safety standard covering minimum testing requirements, vehicle design, and data sharing. Under its preferred system, the federal government would continue setting vehicle safety standards, while states would govern road rules and cities would handle local concerns like curb space, law enforcement, and emergency response. The disagreements emerge in the details. In Washington, DC, Waymo said it broadly supports Councilmember Charles Allen’s effort to establish a regulatory framework allowing commercial robotaxi service, including its goals of funding transit and helping workers transition as transportation becomes more automated. But it objects to parts of the current proposal. Waymo said a 200-vehicle limit would probably be too small for a city the size of Washington. It could accept starting small, but wants regulators to let fleets grow as companies demonstrate safe performance rather than putting a permanent ceiling into law. “I don’t think legislation needs to set a hard cap on that,” Kintz said, “or it’s going to lead to preventing important groups from being able to access the service when they need it.” The company has been more receptive to the proposed 15-cent fee for every mile an autonomous vehicle travels. Kintz said Waymo supports “the fundamental principle of raising revenue” for transit and affected workers, though it raised concerns that a per-mile charge could become prohibitively expensive, particularly for smaller AV operators. But research has also suggested that robotaxis could replace some trips that otherwise would have been taken on public transit, potentially undermining ridership rather than complementing it. On labor, Waymo argues that automation will eliminate some tasks while creating others. “These cars don’t clean, charge, fix themselves, code themselves,” Kintz said, pointing to jobs including fleet technicians, mechanics, remote support workers, and operations managers. Of course, simply taking the driver out of the driver’s seat could have huge economic implications. Earlier this month, Uber said that 10.2 million drivers and couriers earned money on its platform during the second quarter.  [Image: An Amazon-owned Zoox driverless robotaxi drives down a street on August 3rd in San Francisco. The National Highway Traffic Safety ‌Administration cleared Amazon-owned Zoox robotaxis to charge customers for robotaxi rides. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gettyimages-2288941257.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Kintz acknowledged that autonomous vehicles could eventually displace drivers and said Waymo was “eyes open” about that possibility. But he argued the change would happen over time and that unions could help build retraining and reskilling programs for affected workers. Asked whether autonomous driving would ultimately create more jobs than it eliminated, Kintz said it was “too soon to tell.” Notably Waymo has continued to expand as these fights play out. The California Public Utilities Commission this month cleared the company to expand driverless passenger service across parts of 18 counties, including Sacramento and San Diego and more of the Los Angeles and Bay Area regions. Kathy Hochul withdrew a proposal earlier this year that would have opened the door to driverless robotaxis outside New York City after taxi drivers, unions, and state lawmakers opposed it. Six months later, commercial driverless service remains illegal in the state, and legalization efforts are stalled. In DC, labor unions are fighting legislation that would legalize commercial robotaxis, while lawmakers are weighing a 200-vehicle cap and a 15-cent-per-mile fee that would fund Metro upgrades and aid workers displaced by autonomous vehicles. A July City Council hearing on the proposal stretched for a grueling 10 hours. In San Francisco, Mayor Daniel Lurie, a vocal supporter of robotaxis, is now calling for tougher robotaxi regulations after Waymos repeatedly snarled traffic during emergencies and major events. And as of July, California police can now formally cite autonomous-vehicle manufacturers when their driverless cars break traffic laws. And while Congress has yet to pass comprehensive robotaxi legislation, federal regulators have stepped up their scrutiny. The Trump administration’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration recently warned autonomous-vehicle companies that vehicles unable to safely interact with police, firefighters, and other first responders pose a danger to the public. Even in states that have broadly welcomed autonomous vehicles, governments are grappling with how to oversee them. Texas this year began enforcing new permitting requirements for commercial AV operators, while cities in Florida have complained that state preemption laws leave them with little power to respond to problems on their own streets. Taxi drivers, labor unions, and safety advocates have fought autonomous vehicles for years. What’s changing is the scale and immediacy of the fight. Now that robotaxis have burst free from the pages of science fiction and onto actual city streets, policymakers are confronting a messier reality filled with questions about safety, regulation, growth, and jobs. They’re having to decide how quickly fleets should be allowed to expand, what companies must prove before they do, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. Waymo, the market leader, is currently operating more than 3,500 vehicles publicly in 11 US cities. It’s testing in a total of 10 cities and plans to extend the Explorer program to Austin and Miami later this year. Tesla, which began its Robotaxi rollout with a safety monitor aboard more than a year ago, appears to finally be growing its unsupervised fleet ahead of launching its purpose-built robotaxi, the Cybercab, later this month. Still, for all the political attention, robotaxis remain a tiny share of the US ridehailing market. At that scale, robotaxis haven’t yet displaced many driving jobs or fundamentally changed how cities move. But their visibility vastly exceeds their market share, especially when a driverless car stops in the wrong place during a blackout or interferes with an emergency response. And the consequences could look very different as autonomous fleets grow from thousands of vehicles to hundreds of thousands. That’s why the battles taking shape across the country are increasingly about the terms of expansion: what companies have to prove before they grow, what they owe cities and workers, and how much control cities and states should have over their operations. It wants multi-stage testing and commercial-deployment permits, under which companies would have to demonstrate their vehicles can operate safely with a small fleet before adding more cars, while continuing to share safety data after commercial service begins. It also wants autonomous vehicles to use multiple kinds of sensors, rather than relying on cameras alone (as Tesla does), and is calling for restrictions on marketing terms like “Autopilot” or “Full Self-Driving” for consumer driver-assist features when the systems still require human oversight. The group isn’t opposed to autonomous vehicles, Sanchez said, but is “pro the safe development of technology.” He added that AV safety isn’t a settled question, and that even a strong record today doesn’t guarantee the same after a software or hardware change. Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), who has pushed for greater federal oversight of AVs, makes a similar argument about transparency. “Autonomous vehicle companies are making huge claims about how their technology is going to save lives,” Markey told The Verge in a statement. “But right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.” Markey has investigated AV companies’ use of remote human operators and introduced legislation that would require them to regularly report safety data. "“Right now, our regulatory structure amounts to this: we hope they’re telling the truth.”" - Sen. Ed Markey “Communities deserve transparency and consistent oversight before we let Big Tech invade their public roads,” he said. But safety is only part of the fight. For labor groups, the stakes are also economic. Peter Finn, Teamsters international vice president at large, called autonomous vehicles an “existential threat” to the work his members do. He pointed to the enormous number of jobs potentially affected by autonomous driving beyond rideshare drivers, including truckers, delivery drivers, and other commercial drivers. Finn said the Teamsters plan to pursue the issue again. “If the technology is solely designed to automate and eliminate labor costs, the only entity benefiting from that is corporations,” Finn said. articles.title: 2 US military refueling aircraft depart Bulgaria amid anger from Iran over deployment
articles.summary: Two U.S. military refueling aircraft departed Bulgaria last week amid Iran’s anger over the planes’ deployment to Bezmer Air Base. Two Air Force KC-135 planes left the air base located in the southeast of Bulgaria on Friday, and the flights they conducted were for training purposes during their deployment, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told…
articles.body:
Two U.S. military refueling aircraft departed Bulgaria last week amid Iran’s anger over the planes’ deployment to Bezmer Air Base.

Two Air Force KC-135 planes left the air base located in the southeast of Bulgaria on Friday, and the flights they conducted were for training purposes during their deployment, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters on Saturday, according to the Bulgarian News Agency.

The U.S. Air Force confirmed the Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, air-to-air refueling tankers, departed Bulgaria to support “other operational requirements.”

“U.S. military aircraft routinely transit and are hosted by Allied and partner nations, including in Bulgaria, in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements,” an Air Force spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill on Monday.

“We are grateful for Bulgaria’s support in regional security and we look forward to our continued partnership, remaining always vigilant in our collective defense,” spokesperson said.

The U.S. asked Bulgaria for temporary deployment of the refueling planes, a request that Iran sharply criticized, stating the Balkan nation would be complicit in “aggression and war crimes.”

Last month, Bulgaria’s Parliament approved the deployment of U.S. aircraft and military personnel to Bezmer Air Base in support of the U.S.’s Operation Epic Fury.

The deployment, which was approved on July 22, would have lasted from July 24 until the end of September.

Bezmer Air Base, which is located about 150 miles southwest of Sofia, is a joint-use facility, meaning whenever the U.S. needs to use it for a new purpose, it needs approval from the Bulgarian Parliament.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in late May that the country would cut the stay of U.S. military aircraft at Sofia’s airport, Vasil Levski Sofia Airport, at the end of June after the Trump administration did not allow a visa-free pass for Bulgarian visitors to the U.S.

articles.title: Marines cancel joint drill with South Korea
articles.summary: The United States canceled a large joint amphibious landing exercise between the Marine Corps and South Korean forces set for September over resource constraints tied to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, Seoul’s military announced Monday. “The U.S. Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong…
articles.body:
The United States canceled a large joint amphibious landing exercise between the Marine Corps and South Korean forces set for September over resource constraints tied to the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, Seoul’s military announced Monday.

“The U.S. Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East,” a spokesperson for the South Korean marine corps told reporters, according to Reuters .

Even with the drill canceled, Washington and Seoul were still consulting on eventually resuming the exercise, they said.

The Pentagon referred The Hill’s questions about the decision to the Marine Corps, which did not immediately respond.

Ssangyong, or “Twin Dragons,” is a biennial exercise that involve U.S. and South Korean marines rehearsing amphibious landings with the use of warships, aircraft and ground forces. It has taken place for decades and involves more than 10,000 marines from both countries.

Its revealed cancellation follows President Trump’s surprise announcement last week to cut back a separate joint military drill with South Korea known as Ulchi Freedom Shield. The exercise, which began Aug. 17 and ended Friday , was slashed from 11 days to five over what Trump claimed was a desire to resume diplomatic talks with North Korea and Seoul’s refusal to help the U.S. in the Iran war.

North Korea, which routinely condemns joint drills between the U.S. and South Korea as provocative and a rehearsal for invasion, has said there are no future plans for talks with Washington.

The drill set for September was previously canceled in Trump’s first term​ under the guise it was too costly and would disrupt his diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un​. The war game was brought back in 2023 under the Biden administration.

articles.title: Alabama attorney general subpoenas OpenAI over Hugging Face incident
articles.summary: Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall (R) issued a subpoena to OpenAI on Monday requesting the company respond to a multistate investigation into the handling of its model breach of technology startup Hugging Face. Marshall announced Monday the investigation is trying to determine whether OpenAI violated Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which seeks to protect consumers…
articles.body:
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall (R) issued a subpoena to OpenAI on Monday requesting the company respond to a multistate invest i gation into the handling of its model breach of technology startup Hugging Face.

Marshall announced Monday the investigation is trying to determine whether OpenAI violated Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, which seeks to protect consumers from deceptive, false or unfair business practices, after two of its models went rogue and hacked into Hugging Face.

The Alabama attorney general’s subpoena requests all of the company’s documents, data and information on the July breach.

This includes every “employee, officer and agent” of the AI firm involved in the breach, along with materials on OpenAI’s discovery or awareness of the hack. The state leader is also requesting information on OpenAI’s safety measures and any concerns around model testing raised by employees.

The subpoena comes nearly three weeks after Marshall and 14 other state attorneys general warned OpenAI to preserve its records on the Hugging Face breach.

OpenAI revealed late last month that two of its models — its latest GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model — were being evaluated in an internal testing sandbox when they breached past the environment and broke into Hugging Face’s database without a human prompt to do so.

The models were being tested for hacking capabilities in an isolated testing environment with constrained network access and had their normal safety checks off as a result, according to the company.

While trying to find a solution for one of the tests, the models exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in a third-party software to gain access to the internet.

From there, the agents accessed another testing environment without authorization before hacking into Hugging Face, which hosts hundreds of thousands of open-source models, datasets and cloud environments.

Disclosing the incident, OpenAI said it found a “small number of cases” in which the models “identified and used publicly exposed credentials at the account-level on other publicly-available services.”

A spokesperson for OpenAI told The Hill the breach “marked an important moment for AI safety.” The company is conducting a thorough review, along with external advisers.

OpenAI said it will release a technical report with “relevant government authorities” and publish the findings publicly following the review.

In a letter earlier this month, the coalition of attorneys general argued that OpenAI failed to confirm the testing environment was secure despite the “severe risks posed by the scenario.”

articles.title: Unexpected GLP-1 side effect? Studies show the meds may help people with addictions
articles.summary: From unexpected babies to “Ozempic teeth,” the ultra-popular class of GLP-1 medications are turning out to have a few unanticipated side effects. Emerging research shows the drugs, which have proven effective in treating obesity and diabetes, may also be useful in treating addiction.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – From unexpected babies to “ Ozempic teeth ,” the ultra-popular class of GLP-1 medications is turning out to have a few unanticipated side effects .

Emerging research shows the drugs , which have proven effective in treating obesity and diabetes, may also be useful in treating addiction.

The medications’ full potential is coming to light as more people are prescribed a GLP-1 , which includes the brand names Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy and Zepbound. As 15 percent of Americans say they’ve tried a GLP-1 , researchers are learning more about how it impacts all aspects of life, not just diet.

“This drug has been available in the medical community since 2005,” said Dr. Eugene Lucas, professor and coordinator of the Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner Program at Wilkes University.

“And over time, when physicians are ordering these medications for people with obesity, diabetes, they’re finding that if they have a concurrent addictive disorder, and specifically alcohol, that they’re either cutting back or stopping their alcohol use,” Lucas added.

A large study of more than 200,000 people in Sweden found using a GLP-1 drug was associated with a decreased risk of hospitalization from alcohol use disorder.

Another study by researchers at the Washington University School of Medicine, which looked at 600,000 veterans with type 2 diabetes, found the medications were tied to a lower risk of developing any kind of substance use disorder.

“In addiction medicine, a lot of treatments target just one thing – for example, a nicotine patch helps with smoking, but not alcohol – but there is no medication that works across addictive substances, let alone all of them,” said the study’s senior author , Dr. Ziyad Al-Aly.

If GLP-1s are able to work across multiple addictions — not just alcohol or one type of drug — they could be a promising treatment path.

Treating addiction is not an FDA-approved use of GLP-1 medication, but Lucas said that could be a possibility down the line if enough research proves it works.

Alcoholism is researched more than other types of substance use, the doctor said.

“The focus has been mostly on alcohol,” he continued. “There have been some studies done on cocaine, methamphetamine, and opioid addiction, but the findings are not conclusive.”

More research is also needed to understand why the drugs meant to treat obesity and diabetes could work to curb smoking, drinking or drug use. Al-Aly said GLP-1s may help with addiction because they target the craving center of the brain.

“It blunts that craving that pulls people toward whatever they’re addicted to,” he said.

“It’s so exciting to see GLP-1s come into this level of the research to say, ‘Hey, this is another tool that we can use to help people, reduce their alcohol intake or reach abstinence from alcohol,’ whatever that goal is,” said Dr. Samuel Parish, an addiction medicine specialist, told Nexstar’s WCBD . “But at this moment, we can’t say with certainty.”

Another study by researchers at the Washington University School of Medicine, which looked at 600,000 veterans with type 2 diabetes, found the medications were tied to a lower risk of developing any kind of substance use disorder.

“In addiction medicine, a lot of treatments target just one thing – for example, a nicotine patch helps with smoking, but not alcohol – but there is no medication that works across addictive substances, let alone all of them,” said the study’s senior author , Dr. Ziyad Al-Aly.
If GLP-1s are able to work across multiple addictions — not just alcohol or one type of drug — they could be a promising treatment path.
Treating addiction is not an FDA-approved use of GLP-1 medication, but Lucas said that could be a possibility down the line if enough research proves it works.
Alcoholism is researched more than other types of substance use, the doctor said.
“The focus has been mostly on alcohol,” he continued. “There have been some studies done on cocaine, methamphetamine, and opioid addiction, but the findings are not conclusive.”

More research is also needed to understand why the drugs meant to treat obesity and diabetes could work to curb smoking, drinking or drug use. Al-Aly said GLP-1s may help with addiction because they target the craving center of the brain.
“It blunts that craving that pulls people toward whatever they’re addicted to,” he said.

“It’s so exciting to see GLP-1s come into this level of the research to say, ‘Hey, this is another tool that we can use to help people, reduce their alcohol intake or reach abstinence from alcohol,’ whatever that goal is,” said Dr. Samuel Parish, an addiction medicine specialist, told Nexstar’s WCBD . “But at this moment, we can’t say with certainty.”

articles.title: US military launches first known drug boat strike in months, killing 2 ‘narco-terrorists’
articles.summary: The U.S. military launched its first known strike on an alleged drug boat in two months off the coast of Latin America on Sunday, killing two “narco-terrorists” in the eastern Pacific. The U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) said early Monday the “low-profile” vessel operated along “established narco-trafficking routes” in the eastern Pacific and intelligence “confirmed” the…
articles.body:
The U.S. military launched its first known strike on an alleged drug boat in two months off the coast of Latin America on Sunday, killing two “narco-terrorists” in the eastern Pacific.

The U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) said early Monday the “low-profile” vessel operated along “established narco-trafficking routes” in the eastern Pacific and intelligence “confirmed” the boat’s involvement in “narco-trafficking.”

“We are committed to imposing total systemic friction on narco-terrorists — disrupting their operations, dismantling their leadership and eliminating cartel terror across the region,” Southcom Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said.

The U.S. military began the lethal boat strike campaign in early September last year, targeting alleged drug-trafficking boats in both the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean.

The Sunday attack was the first publicly disclosed strike since June 21, when the U.S. military said it killed eight “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean. Since Sept. 2 last year, the military has conducted a minimum of 67 strikes and killed at least 223 “narco-terrorists.”

Top U.S. officials have said the campaign is waged in part to cut off the flow of illicit drugs in the region. Law-of-war experts have panned the attacks as illegal extrajudicial killings.

Earlier this month, Southcom announced a new military unit , dubbed Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, intended to broaden the Pentagon’s war against drugs on the continent in collaboration with partners and allies in the region.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the U.S.-led countercartel coalition in Panama earlier this month, as the Pentagon ramps up its fight against drug cartels in Central and South America.

The Pentagon chief said the motto for the coalition, which Colombia and Honduras recently joined, will be, “We do bad things to bad people.”

articles.title: 3rd person dies from flesh-eating bacteria in Florida
articles.summary: At least two deaths caused by Vibriosis have been reported each year in Florida since 2017.
articles.body:
TAMPA, Fla. ( WFLA ) – Recently updated data from the Florida Department of Health (FDOH) shows that another person has died in the state from the flesh-eating bacteria Vibrio vulnificus.

The most recent death marks the third in less than a month , as total cases continue to rise across the Gulf Coast region.

As of August 15, there were 17 confirmed cases of the disease in 12 Florida counties: Bay, Brevard, Broward, Hillsborough, Lee, Marion, Miami-Dade, Okaloosa, Palm Beach, Polk, Santa Rosa and St. Johns.

The latest death was reported in Bay County, where two people had been diagnosed with Vibriosis, one between the ages of 35 and 39 and one between the ages of 55 and 59.

The data does not clarify which patient died, nor does it include any other details about the victims, such as whether they had any pre-existing diseases or immune vulnerabilities.

The bacteria occur naturally in warm, brackish seawater, and most people get sick from eating raw or undercooked shellfish . There is also a risk of infection if an open wound is exposed to seawater.

In the Sunshine State, cases tend to spike after hurricanes or other strong storms that leave standing water, FDOH said.

There were 82 cases and 19 deaths in 2024, likely related to Hurricanes Helene and Milton . In 2025, that number dropped sharply to 33 total cases and 5 deaths.

At least two deaths caused by Vibriosis have been reported each year in Florida since 2017, data shows.
