articles.title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
articles.summary: The ‘Hochulization’ tool purports to subvert proposed gun-blocking 3D printer software.
articles.body: The creator of the world’s first 3D-printed gun claims he’s developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It’s an opening volley in what’s shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of ghost guns and individuals trying to create workarounds. Cody Wilson, who claims to have made the detection-defying tool, is calling it “Hochulization” as a direct jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who pushed through the nation’s first law mandating gun file detection software on new printers earlier this year. “New York is trying to reach into the internet and police how open-source 3D printing is done,” Wilson, who’s based out of Austin, Texas, told The Verge. “I think of it as a self-defense measure.” The tool is designed to break a relatively simple approach to a 3D-printed gun ban. Wilson’s company, Defense Distributed, runs DEFCAD, the world’s largest 3D gun file repository, which he says hosts over 200,000 files of gun designs and components, such as suppressors. Each of those files can be identified by a hash, a unique string of numbers that’s created by running the file through an algorithm. In theory, a gun file detection system that uses a hashing-based identification method would look for those exact hashes to determine whether a file is a potential gun, flag it, and prevent it from printing. Hochulization mucks up that process by automatically changing those hashes. It adds a series of bytes to each file that changes the hash without altering the function of the end product. A 3D-printed suppressor or gun, in other words, would still work as intended. “Hochulizaiton is a de minimis policy to change the hash of every file that gets created and downloaded to where there is never going to be a complete library of hashes,” Wilson says. Wilson says he wants to apply the Hochulization treatment to all files hosted on DEFCAD by default as a means of “self-defense” against growing calls for gun detection software, which he describes as invasive digital surveillance. Wilson says he will make the tool available to DEFCAD users, though he says he also intends to make it open source, which would let an individual user with a gun file apply the tool to scramble the hash and potentially sidestep detection. [Image: Image: Cody Wilson https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_9601.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] “I think all the files in the repository, the 3D files anyway, should be Hochulized,” he adds. “And so that is what we’ll do.” He claims he has begun this process. Wilson’s approach is an early indicator of the resistance to 3D-print-blocking tech. In this case, the momentum is coming from a Second Amendment advocate, but that might not always be the case. Groups of makers, digital rights experts, and members of the entertainment industry who aren’t focused on guns have all spoken out against the tech, expressing fears that requiring file scanning on printers introduces a new level of digital surveillance into the process that could limit what everyone can create. 3D-printed firearms are growing in number but remain an evolving public threat. In 2021, the New York Police Department confiscated just one 3D-printed gun. That jumped to 109 in 2024. Prominent gun policy group Everytown found similar upticks across 20 other cities. Still, when compared with the percentage of conventional firearms confiscated around the country, 3D-printed models remain comparatively small. The total number of firearms in the US has been estimated to outnumber people. But 3D-printed gun technology has also come a long way since Wilson first printed his single-shot “Liberator” in 2013. Today, models like the FGC-9 can fire multiple high-velocity rounds without breaking and have been found in the hands of neo-Nazi cells in Europe and rebel groups fighting Myanmar’s military junta. 3D-printed gun components, like switches that can turn a single-fire conventional firearm into a machine gun or suppressors that make shots easier to conceal, are arguably even more dangerous. These tools are typically illegal or require special licenses to acquire. 3D printing offers a workaround. Luigi Mangione, who admitted to shooting and killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and is awaiting sentencing, allegedly used a partially 3D-printed Glock-style pistol frame and a 3D-printed suppressor. Policymakers and gun control advocates argue cases like this demonstrate a glaring gap in the legal system. People with prior felony convictions and others who aren’t legally allowed to own guns can do so anyway with the help of a 3D printer. And while many states regulate the making and selling of so-called “ghost guns,” actually enforcing those laws is notoriously difficult. This new approach, which requires 3D printers to install mandatory file-blocking software, attempts to close that gap by stopping a print before it ever starts. Industry experts are still debating whether that’s technically feasible at scale. Gov. Hochul, who pushed through the country’s first law mandating print-blocking software on new printers as part of the state’s FY 2027 budget, says it’s necessary to close what she calls a black-market “plastic pipeline.” Hochul’s office did not respond to our request for comment regarding Wilson’s Hochulization workaround. New York isn’t alone. A similar bill in California, AB 2047, is gaining momentum and is advancing to the Senate floor for a vote. Like in New York, this bill would require new printers manufactured or sold in the state to be equipped with print-blocking software. The state Department of Justice would publish a roster of compliant printer models, and those not on the list would be banned from sale or transfer in the state starting in December 2029. A spokesperson for California Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, who introduced and coauthored AB 2047, declined to comment when asked about Wilson’s project. Neither of these efforts explicitly details what print-blocking software should look like. That’s being left up to groups of industry experts with backgrounds in manufacturing technology, artificial intelligence, firearms regulation, and other relevant fields. A purely hash-matching approach would limit the number of non-guns mistakenly identified as guns, but as Wilson’s project shows, it may be trivially easy to bypass. More expansive approaches that use AI to analyze a file’s geometry and predict whether it’s a gun would almost certainly prevent more guns from being printed, but they also risk introducing more false positives. Wilson’s hoping his tool will make its way into those working group conversations. By showing just how simple it is to complicate a purely hashing-based approach, he’s essentially trying to force policymakers’ hands into choosing between a more aggressive scanning scheme or the status quo of nothing.  “You are going to have to do more than create a database of known files and check against hashes because that’s too easy to defeat,” Wilson says.  Dartmouth College associate professor of engineering Solomon Diamond told The Verge Hochulization would likely work on a technical level to bypass a hash-based detection model. Still, he said that doesn’t necessarily make the approach useless as a policy path. In reality, it’s not clear that every 3D printer user would go the extra step to change a hash. Downloading gun files from DEFCAD also requires setting up an account and linking an email address, which is another barrier to entry. The hashing approach, in other words, is better than nothing and might stop the casual, less motivated user from downloading a gun. Moving beyond hash matching, Wilson says his team found other ways to bypass more sophisticated detection using “adversarial noise.” To do this, his team first created their own AI detection model designed to classify guns and gun parts, trained partly on both public and non-public files from DEFCAD’s database. They based their model on claims made by other companies, such as the Spain-based Print&Go, which is working with lawmakers in New York and California. Wilson claims he was able to get files past their own system using techniques like re-saving the same gun part as a slightly different mesh (a digital representation of the object’s surface) or adding “a small extra lump of unused geometry.” Overall, Wilson says their gun detection system, even when trained on high-quality data, still had a 30 percent false positive rate. He says that false positives speak to issues inherent to more prediction-based systems.  Wilson approaches the scanning debate as a self-described crypto-anarchist and an aggressive Second Amendment advocate. He’s a leading voice in arguing that gun files should be considered constitutionally protected speech under the First Amendment. He also created the platform Hatreon as an alternative to Patreon to thwart its speech policies, a platform that attracted extremists, white supremacists, and neo-Nazis until it was shut down in 2018. But concerns over this proposed change to the way 3D printing works aren’t limited to gun owners. Makers and hobbyists previously told The Verge they fear this new paradigm will falsely label non-guns, like this e-reader case, as dangerous weapons and limit their freedom of expression in the process. Others are concerned a process that earnestly starts with gun file increments could be expanded by corporations looking to enforce IP and copyright protections. Wilson isn’t new when it comes to picking fights over 3D-printed gun laws. After posting the first Liberator files online, the State Department ordered him to remove them and threatened him with jail time for allegedly violating ITAR export-control rules. Wilson and Defense Distributed sued the agency, claiming they attempted to stop him from publishing computer code, which he says is constitutionally protected under the First Amendment. That set in motion a complex web of legal fights over the broad claim that the gun file codes aren’t constitutionally protected speech, an issue that’s still being debated in courts.

articles.title: Nevada sues Trump administration over Colorado River water use cuts
articles.summary: The state of Nevada is suing the federal government over its plans for Colorado River water use reductions, saying its cuts are too steep. Nevada sued Monday after the federal government finalized its 10-year framework for planned cuts on Friday. The Colorado River provides water for agricultural, municipal and industrial uses for seven states in the…
articles.body:
The state of Nevada is suing the federal government over its plans for Colorado River water use reductions, saying its cuts are too steep.

Nevada sued Monday after the federal government finalized its 10-year framework for planned cuts on Friday.

The Colorado River provides water for agricultural, municipal and industrial uses for seven states in the Western U.S., including Nevada.

The federal government’s plan details cuts for Nevada, Arizona and California, known collectively as the Lower Basin states.

Nevada said in its court filing Monday that the plan could cause the state to lose as much as 71 percent of its Colorado River water allocation — and that this would threaten health and safety, the environment and the economy in the southern part of the state.

“This isn’t about political posturing; this is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy,” Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) said in a statement.

He lamented that Upper Basin states — Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming — “are not required to contribute a drop.”

The Interior Department declined The Hill’s request for comment.

In the past, the Trump administration has described the 10-year plan as a flexible framework meant to respond to changing water conditions in the river.

The government imposed this plan after the states that rely on the river were not able to come up with their own agreement for cutting water use.

Over the last quarter century, the Colorado River has faced a drought that has lessened the availability of water on the river. This drought has been exacerbated by climate change and water overuse.

Nevada, in its court challenge, has asked a federal court in the state to toss the plan, saying that the federal government did not follow adequate procedures.

Specifically, it alleged that the government did not correctly apply the Law of the River, failed to consider a reasonable range of alternatives and did not adequately consider the plan’s environmental impacts, among other issues.

articles.title: Hegseth: Economic pressure hurts Iranian regime ‘the most’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that the Trump administration’s economic pressure on Iran is hurting the regime “the most right now” but did not rule out the U.S. military resuming airstrikes if necessary. “If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that the Trump administration’s economic pressure on Iran is hurting the regime “the most right now” but did not rule out the U.S. military resuming airstrikes if necessary.

“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we’ll do what we need to do,” Hegseth told reporters in Oshkosh, Wis., as part of the Pentagon’s Arsenal of Freedom tour. “But economic pressure hurts them the most right now.”

The Pentagon chief’s remarks came hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previewed the new economic pressure campaign against Tehran as the conflict has reached a stalemate after six months of hostilities.

Bessent warned countries to cut off any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system, discussing the new Operation Economic Outcast but offering few specifics.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent told a reporter Monday when asked about specifics.

The Treasury secretary said President Trump is making calls to world leaders while officials from the Defense, Treasury and State departments are connecting with their counterparts and demanding action in severing ties with Iran.

“I would expect that very quickly, if they do not respond, then you will see the ramifications of their actions,” Bessent said.

Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran’s parliamentary speaker, fired back Monday at the U.S. over the rollout of the economic pressure campaign.

“Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,” Qalibaf wrote on social media .

“Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere,” the Iranian official continued.

Hegseth, meanwhile, told reporters Monday that the application of more economic pressure ensures that the “only choice” Iran has is “to come to the table and actually talk about their nuclear program, which is what the president has demanded.”

The Defense secretary touted the U.S. naval blockade and claimed that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz.

“Iran can’t run anything through; we can. The world economy realizes that, and so they made a big bet on controlling it, and they can’t,” Hegseth told reporters.

Five vessels crossed the strait on Sunday, lower than the 25 successful crossings on Saturday and 21 on Friday, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler .

The U.S. military has redirected 71 commercial ships, disabled three and boarded another two since resuming the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea, the U.S. Central Command wrote on social media Monday. More than 40 vessels carrying humanitarian aid have been allowed to pass.

“Ultimately, their economy is in a spiral,” Hegseth said. “They also know that we control the Strait of Hormuz, that our blockade is ironclad, and that oil is flowing through, ultimately.”

articles.title: Senate Democrats call for hearing on Iran war’s strain on troops
articles.summary: Nearly all Senate Armed Services Committee minority members on Monday called on the panel’s head to hold a hearing with Pentagon leadership to discuss the impact extended deployments in support of the Iran war are having on U.S. service members. The letter — led by Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and signed by 11 other senators…
articles.body:
Nearly all Senate Armed Services Committee minority members on Monday called on the panel’s head to hold a hearing with Pentagon leadership to discuss the impact extended deployments in support of the Iran war are having on U.S. service members.

The letter — led by Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and signed by 11 other senators — was addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), the Senate Armed Services Committee’s chair, and highlighted the panel’s responsibility to make sure the U.S. military is “properly led, well-resourced, supported and able to conduct its missions.”

“Recent reports of sailors suffering from severe mental health issues amid deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln have only added to a disturbing pattern of failures to adequately plan and support our troops, who have been away from their families indefinitely as the Iran War drags on,” the senators wrote .

The Democrats demanded that Wicker hold a public hearing with Defense Department officials to explain to Congress and the public how the extended deployments impact military readiness and how it plans to sustain soldiers, sailors and airmen in the war indefinitely as the Trump administration struggles to find an off-ramp to the conflict.

A growing number of voices are demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding the toll the Iran war is taking on service members following damning reports of low morale and mental health crises aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been deployed since November.

The strike group was originally intended to return home in May but was redirected to the Middle East in January ahead of the Iran war and has now been deployed for more than 260 days — including more than 200 consecutive days without a port call.

Earlier this month, family members of those aboard told several outlets they had received urgent messages about food and water shortages on the ship, broken plumbing, exhaustion and mental health issues serious enough that multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard.

Administration officials quickly went on the defensive, insisting the media had falsely portrayed the conditions aboard but relayed that the strike group would soon be relieved by the USS George Washington aircraft carrier.

In Monday’s letter, the 12 senators said the strain on service members is not just confined to the Navy, and that their offices and members of the media “have heard story after story of Soldiers and Airmen, including National Guardsmen and Reservists, seeing their deployments extended with uncertainty about when they will be relieved by other units and can return home to their families.”

They also said bases in the Middle East originally designed to support a specific number of troops “have been stretched to support a much larger scale of units now stationed there — and conditions are deteriorating as too many people meet too little space and supplies.”

The strain on troops is “unconscionable,” the lawmakers wrote.

“Troops are suffering because of this Administration’s inability to end this war or make the environment safe enough for our servicemembers to be delivered the food, medication or supplies they need,” the senators continued. “All these developments strongly indicate a systemic failure of planning and adaptation by the Secretary of Defense” and senior Defense Department leaders.

The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is in a stalemate after diplomatic efforts fell apart earlier this summer. Tehran has now withstood nearly seven months of U.S. military attacks, initially in coordination with Israel.

Washington has opted to instead try to strangle Tehran economically to bring about peace, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issuing a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

The U.S. already has imposed a naval blockade against Tehran in the Strait of Hormuz which has severely diminished the amount of Iranian oil exported by sea.

articles.title: FDA approves new blood test for Alzheimer’s disease
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted approval for a new test for Alzheimer’s disease, marking the fourth time such a blood test has been approved in less than two years. Roche announced Sunday that the FDA had granted approval to its Elecsys Phospho-Tau blood test for diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease. It’s the fourth such…
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted approval for a new test for Alzheimer’s disease , marking the fourth time such a blood test has been approved in less than two years.

Roche announced Sunday that the FDA had granted approval to its Elecsys Phospho-Tau blood test for diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease. It’s the fourth such test to be granted FDA approval after the first was given the green light in May 2025 .

Developed in collaboration with Eli Lilly, the test is intended for people 55 years and older with “signs, symptoms, or complaints of cognitive decline.” The test may help physicians identify patients who should be considered for further evaluation earlier, according to Roche.

“FDA clearance of Elecsys pTau217 marks an important milestone in Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis and underscores Roche’s continued leadership in advancing innovative solutions that can help patients get answers sooner,” Dan Malarek, president and CEO of Roche Diagnostics North America, said in a company press release.

“As the first and only FDA-cleared, single-biomarker blood test supporting both rule-in and rule-out assessment of amyloid pathology, Elecsys pTau217 has the potential to transform how Alzheimer’s is assessed across primary and specialty care,” Malarek added.

Alzheimer’s disease is commonly diagnosed through cognitive testing, brain scans and by ruling out other conditions that could be causing issues with cognition and memory.

The Alzheimer’s Association celebrated the approval in a statement Monday. The organization emphasized that no single test can diagnose Alzheimer’s alone, but developments like this new approval can be incorporated with other standard evaluation methods.

“Each FDA clearance gives clinicians another validated option to work with when evaluating patients showing signs of cognitive impairment,” said Maria C. Carrillo, chief science officer of the Alzheimer’s Association. “That’s real progress for a field that, for decades, had far too few tools to offer.”

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln headed for port in Thailand after 250 days at sea
articles.summary: Sailors and crew members on the USS Abraham Lincoln, which recently departed the Middle East after being stationed in the region as part of the U.S. conflict with Iran, have a port call scheduled after 250 days at sea, USA Today reported Monday, citing family members. Texts to the outlet said the Lincoln planned to…
articles.body:
Sailors and crew members on the USS Abraham Lincoln, which recently departed the Middle East after being stationed in the region as part of the U.S. conflict with Iran, have a port call scheduled after 250 days at sea, USA Today reported Monday , citing family members.

Texts to the outlet said the Lincoln planned to stop in Thailand in early September after its extended deployment. One sailor told a relative to send hotel ideas that looked good in Thailand, while another told her family member that she was excited after having talked about visiting Thailand.

The Hill has reached out to the U.S. Navy for comment.

Reports of the port call came days after the USS George Washington, the aircraft carrier intended to relieve the Lincoln, arrived in the Middle East , leaving the U.S. without a carrier in Asia.

Multiple media reports noted deteriorating conditions aboard the Lincoln in the weeks leading up to its departure from the Middle East, including rotting food and mental health concerns among crew members.

Family members of those aboard said they received urgent messages about food and water shortages and mental health issues serious enough that several sailors attempted to jump overboard.

The aircraft carrier departed San Diego in November. The strike group was originally intended to return home in May but was redirected to the Middle East in January ahead of the Iran war, and it was deployed for more than 260 days — including more than 200 consecutive days without a port call.

Most of the Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee have called for a hearing with Pentagon leadership to discuss the impact of extended deployments in support of the Iran war on U.S. service members, including on the Lincoln.

“Recent reports of sailors suffering from severe mental health issues amid deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln have only added to a disturbing pattern of failures to adequately plan and support our troops, who have been away from their families indefinitely as the Iran War drags on,” Democratic Senators wrote in a letter to committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.).

President Trump and other administration officials have dismissed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, claiming them to be false.

The conflict with Iran has been locked in a stalemate, with the Trump administration announcing new sanctions of a scale and severity akin to the U.S. landing on Normandy Beach during World War II, calling the new economic warfare on Iran “Economic D-Day.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

articles.title: ‘Don’t be a loser’: Robert Kiyosaki sounds alarm on $40T US debtload — warns owners of this ‘fake asset’ will get poorer
articles.summary: “People who are financially uneducated and invest in fake assets get poorer.”
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Robert Kiyosaki has never been shy about issuing dire financial warnings. But with America's national debt reaching a staggering new milestone, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author is turning up the volume.

"$40 TRILLION US NATIONAL [debt] soon!!" Kiyosaki wrote (1) on X. "What are you doing about it?"

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

JPMorgan sees gold hitting $5,000/oz by Q4 — and savvy investors are protecting their wealth with a tax-advantaged Gold IRA. Get your free guide from Priority Gold

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

The warning proved timely. America's national debt has now crossed the $40 trillion threshold, according to data from the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Debt to the Penny (2) database.

Kiyosaki believes the country's growing debt burden will ultimately punish people who depend heavily on cash.

"Remember: Savers of cash are the BIGGEST LOSERS!!!!" he declared.

Days later, Kiyosaki doubled down after the Treasury (3) announced it would at least double the size of certain buyback operations involving longer-dated government debt, raising them from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation.

"PRINTING MORE FAKE $," Kiyosaki wrote (4), characterizing the Treasury's move as "another round of quantitative easing."

He argued that the policy would weaken the U.S. Dollar Index and cause inflation to accelerate — leaving "savers of fake $" as "the biggest losers."

However, it's important to distinguish Kiyosaki's characterization from what the Treasury actually announced. These are liquidity-support buybacks intended to improve trading conditions in portions of the Treasury market. They're not technically the same as quantitative easing, which is conducted by the Federal Reserve and expands the Fed's balance sheet.

Still, Kiyosaki's broader concern is easy to understand, especially given how steadily inflation has eroded the dollar's purchasing power over time.

According to the Inflation Calculator (5) on the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis website, $100 in 2026 has the same purchasing power as just $11.74 did in 1970.

That's right. $100 became less than $12.

"Educated investors who invest in assets that go up in value, such as gold, silver, Bitcoin, some real estate, get richer… while people who are financially uneducated and invest in fake assets get poorer," he wrote.

articles.title: Trump Eyes Renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America in Canada Spat
articles.summary: President Donald Trump threatened to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” escalating his war of words with Canadian officials on Tuesday as an intensifying...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump threatened to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," escalating his war of words with Canadian officials on Tuesday as an intensifying trade fight strains the close economic relationship between the countries.

Lutnick's Intervention in Canada Talks Draws Praise, Blame

Canadians Brace for Economic Pain as 50% US Tariffs Take Effect

Canada Sees Long Trade War With US That May Last Beyond Midterms

Apple Gears Up to Launch Its First New Mac Mini in Two Years

Supreme Court Sides With Trump for Now on Mail Ballot Curbs

"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to (be) doing much business with Ontario any longer," Trump said in a social media post.

Trump's threat is the latest volley in an expanding trade war after negotiations between the countries broke down and the US hit Canada with new tariffs on billions in goods. Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced that Canada will impose counter-tariffs and Trump on Monday also vowed to double the automobile tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts starting next year.

Those auto levies would target the Canadian province of Ontario in particular, where steel and auto production is heavily concentrated. Trump and Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, have exchanged a slew of insults and threats.

Earlier: 'Flunky,' 'Loser': Trump Trades Wild Insults With Canada's Ford

Ford has also talked about retaliation against the US, such as cutting off electricity exports.

Trump's threat to rename the iconic Great Lake on the border between the US and Canada echoes his early 2025 move to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

articles.summary: Anti-abortion groups and other conservatives largely applauded the White House announcement that President Trump would nominate health policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner, viewing her as their champion for, among other things, bringing an end to medication abortion. But others in the conservative world were less thrilled. Overton is not…
articles.body:
Anti-abortion groups and other conservatives largely applauded the White House announcement that President Trump would nominate health policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner, viewing her as their champion for, among other things, bringing an end to medication abortion.

But others in the conservative world were less thrilled. Overton is not a favorite of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, whose proponents see her as an obstacle to their goals.

Alex Clark , a MAHA podcaster, told her followers to press their senators against confirming Overton, citing her involvement in an executive order earlier this year that boosted production of glyphosate herbicides, something the MAHA movement is staunchly against.

Clark, in a series of posts on social platform X, said Overton “wrote” the executive order and “has EXTENSIVE personal ties to Bayer,” referring to the pharmaceutical and biotech giant that produces many herbicides.

“Everyone knows she is the biggest roadblock in the admin when it comes to getting several true MAHA initiatives done,” Clark said of Overton. Several unnamed sources said the same in a story about Overton in The Atlantic last month.

Clark’s fervor provoked a White House spokesperson, Kush Desai , to push back online.

“Anyone suggesting that Heidi wrote this EO [executive order], has ties to Bayer, or isn’t MAHA has no clue what they’re talking about,” Desai said. “Pretty much every MAHA win by this Administration absolutely would not have been possible without Heidi often singlehandedly running interagency policy processes.”

Clark dug further in, saying “MAHA moms are smarter than this” and arguing that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is “the most capable fighter we have” but that he’s surrounded by people who “share none of his values.”

The divisions over Overton show an area of friction between the MAHA and the anti-abortion wings of Trump’s coalition. That’s significant as Republicans and the White House look to shore up their base in advance of the midterms and 2028 because both groups are passionate sectors of Trump’s support and risking either is dangerous for Republicans going forward.

Anti-abortion conservatives, for the most part, have been rooting for the administration’s agenda since the beginning, although some have expressed disappointment at what they see as a lack of progress. They’re pushing Trump to crack down further on mifepristone and permanently strip federal funding from Planned Parenthood.

Overton’s appointment is a signal to those anti-abortion advocates that the administration is still moving toward those goals. Overton has denounced abortion and called for more restrictions on prescribing mifepristone. That’s especially relevant as the FDA is currently reviewing the safety of the drug.

Anti-abortion groups lauded Overton’s promotion last week.

“She has the scientific and medical background that will enable her to perform an objective analysis of the dangers chemical abortion poses to women,” John Mize , CEO of Americans United for Life, said in a statement .

Lila Rose , president of Live Action, congratulated Overton in a post on X .

“This is a chance to restore trust and put health over politics,” Rose said. “Dr. Overton should pull the deadly abortion pill from the market. Step one: end mail-order abortions that kill babies even in pro-life states.”

There were other Republican voices against Overton for different reasons. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate committee that will process Overton’s nomination, said he had “strong concerns” about her stance on childhood vaccine recommendations, which has been a sticking point between Cassidy, also a medical doctor, and the administration.

Overton stood next to Trump at a recent ceremony where he signed an executive order paring down the childhood vaccine recommendations. In that, she is aligned with the MAHA movement and Kennedy.

Conservative commentator Laura Loomer also spoke out against Overton, alleging Overton was involved in Health and Human Services’s (HHS) “MAHA Report,” which came out last May and was soon discovered to contain thousands of fake citations .

“Now that Heidi Overton has been selected as the head of the FDA, I’ll remind everyone that she was one of the officials involved in the publication of the notorious and highly embarrassing White House ‘MAHA report’, which was full of fake and AI citations,” Loomer said in a post .

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

The next step in the Republican midterm strategy: hype.

Republicans will be looking to harness pep rally-style hype, viral moments and strong party unity at the Republican National Committee (RNC) convention in Dallas in a few weeks. The event is the first of its kind: in a normal cycle, national party conventions like this are held every four years as a chance to crown a presidential nominee.

But this is not a normal cycle. Republicans are seeing polls that point against them in races down the ballot and around the country as Trump’s approval ratings remain low. In primary elections all over, Democratic voters have turned out in swarms while many Republicans have stayed home.

Republicans are hoping to course-correct with a rousing rally in a key Senate battleground. A GOP strategist told me that the goal is to “build enthusiasm” for the election and remind voters of the stakes if Republicans lose their majorities in Congress, pitching it as “common-sense versus communism.”

Neil Newhouse , Republican strategist and partner at Public Opinion Strategies, told me by email that news of the convention doesn’t seem to have broken through to voters much yet. There are few details about what will happen there besides a website with a list of potential speakers that includes Trump, most of his Cabinet, and a handful of governors, members of Congress, and other prominent MAGA World names.

But if the convention can create some steam to power the Republican message into November, Newhouse said it could be useful.

“To the extent that this convention can reach some of these disaffected or disinterested GOP faithful and reinforce what’s at stake in this election, that could make a significant difference on election day,” Newhouse said.

The stated goals of the convention, according to the website, are as follows: celebrating “the America First agenda” as Trump has enacted it thus far in his term; christening “the American comeback” by “recognizing hardworking Americans … whose work is driving economic growth, advancing energy dominance, and ushering in a new Golden Age of American prosperity”; and celebrating the 250th anniversary of the United States.

Douglas Heye , a former RNC chair and Republican strategist, told me he’s looking to hear more about the agenda for the convention. Although novel, he said, he sees the appeal of the event.

“The idea isn’t a bad one — that it’s not been done before is not a concern, trying something different given historical midterm trends could be helpful, especially for fundraising,” Heye said.

It’s no coincidence that this will all go down at the American Airlines Center in Dallas. Texas’s Senate race between state Attorney General Ken Paxton , who has Trump’s endorsement, and state legislator James Talarico is one of the most expensive and closely watched Senate contests in history.

The timing is also strategic. The two-day event will run Sept. 9-10, right as primaries end and before early voting for November’s general election begins.

RANCHERS VS. TRUMP SHOWDOWN IN OKLAHOMA GOVERNOR’S RACE

Republican voters in Oklahoma will decide Tuesday between Mike Mazzei , Trump’s pick for the next governor, and state Attorney General Gentner Drummond , a rancher. The contest comes amid a furious few days where Republicans of all stripes criticized the White House for lowering import tariffs on foreign beef at the expense of American ranchers.

Drummond on Sunday joined the chorus of Republicans saying Trump was “wrong” to lower tariffs on beef.

“I do think the majority of Oklahomans would agree that the tariffs are too far, that importing cheap beef only injures Oklahoma’s cattlemen, ranchers and farmers,” Drummond told NewsNation.

Trump announced last week that he would temporarily allow more foreign beef into the U.S. at a lower price for importers, an attempt to bring down the cost of a grocery staple as “affordability” looms decisively above the November midterms. But Republican lawmakers and MAGA commentators alike were quick to push back.

“I’ve advised President Trump against this course of action for a year because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them – most of whom are MAGA Republicans,” Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) said on X .

The Republican runoff for the Oklahoma governor’s mansion will be, in some ways, a test of how powerful Trump’s endorsement is for Oklahoma primary voters, especially against a high-profile state official like Drummond. Five of Trump’s picks for gubernatorial races have already lost primaries this summer.

Sept. 4-6: The inaugural Italian version of the Conservative Political Action Conference convenes a leadership summit, gala and other events in Rome. U.S. conservative leaders, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , and other high-profile officials from Europe and the U.S. are among the special guests. Details here .

Sept. 16: American Conservation Coalition, Discipulus Ventures and the Foundation for American Innovation host The New Industrial Age Forum, underwritten by Google, Lockheed Martin, Amazon and others. The goal is to “plan the restoration of America’s industrial independence,” with a focus on tech and AI. Details here .

The USA has assumed leadership of the Geneva Consensus Declaration secretariat, a coalition of 42 nations dedicated to affirming that there is no international right to an abortion and translating that into policy in signer countries. It will be housed under HHS’s Office of Global Affairs and Director Bethany Kozma . More here .

A Florida school board whose longstanding conservative majority had the backing of Gov. Ron DeSantis and Moms for Liberty flipped to a progressive majority last week. The district had been seen as a microcosm of school board culture wars. More here .

Alex Jones will still need to pay more than $1 billion to families of victims of the Sandy Hook shooting after courts in Connecticut and Texas judged the Infowars founder responsible for defamation as he spread conspiracy theories about the shooting. More here .

articles.title: French has become a sticking point in the Canada-US trade dispute. Here’s why
articles.summary: As a trade war between the United States and Canada looms following the collapse of talks last week, a key issue has emerged: French language laws.
articles.body:
As a trade war between the United States and Canada looms following the collapse of talks last week, a key issue has emerged that's further inflamed tensions between the longtime allies: French language laws.

Canada is a bilingual country and has laws protecting both of its official languages: English and French, the first language spoken for roughly one fifth of the population, including nearly 85% of primarily Francophone province of Quebec.

Among the laws, product labels must be displayed in both English and French, and US streaming platforms must support and promote Canadian content (including Indigenous and French Canadian content) to audiences north of the border.

Canada's language requirements have long been viewed by the US as a trade barrier but are generally a red line for Ottawa — which Prime Minister Mark Carney enforced by walking away from a deal which he said included "threats to French language and culture."

On Monday, Carney said Canada "could not accept" the proposed deal that would have weakened French language protections, telling reporters that his government "will not give (the US) what they have asked."

Many in Canada have rallied behind Carney's decision — and particularly his comments about protecting French culture, a core part of Canada's national identity.

After US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called Ottawa's concerns about French a "funny, fake story" on Monday, the Canadian leader denied the issue was a laughing matter, saying there is an "enormous gap between our perspective and the US perspective."

"For Americans, French language, Francophone culture, Canadian culture, these are irritants," Carney said in French at a news conference in Lévis, Quebec.

"Here in Quebec, here in Canada, these are rights," he said, as a group of reporters applauded.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump denied that the US wanted to interfere with Canada's French language laws and accused Carney of using the issue to score political points in Quebec in a post to Truth Social.

"I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing. This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec," the US president posted.

His post came the same day Canada announced tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on over 700 American goods, including reciprocal 50% duties on US steel and aluminum, set to take effect September 8.

articles.title: Callaway apologizes for ‘Good Good’ ad showing woman shoved to ground
articles.summary: Golf company Callaway is apologizing for an advertisement for a new driver posted by its media partner Good Good Golf that depicted violence against women and was subsequently taken down. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer said the video, which was posted over the weekend on Good Good Golf social channels,…
articles.body:
Golf company Callaway is apologizing for an advertisement for a new driver posted by its media partner Good Good Golf that depicted violence against women and was subsequently taken down.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer said the video, which was posted over the weekend on Good Good Golf social channels, was approved by Callaway and said it should not have been.

“Mistakes were made,” Brewer said, adding the company is still investigating how the advertisement, which he said does not reflect the company’s values, was approved.

The ad in question was promoting a new Good Good Golf quantum driver Callaway is rolling out this week.

It shows a woman, a member of the Good Good Golf content team, reaching for the driver when the company’s co-founder, Garrett Clark, rushes after her and knocks her to the ground.

“Don’t touch my driver,” Clark angrily says in the video while standing over her.

Following widespread backlash online, Good Good Golf took the video down and apologized for its content.

“Good Good has always stood for making the game more inclusive for all and we will continue to ensure that is our mission moving forward,” the company said.

Callaway did not say if it was reviewing its partnership with Good Good Golf but insisted “it will learn from this and do better.”

articles.title: Ray Dalio says the US faces a debt crisis ‘in three years, give or take two.’ 5 things Americans can do now
articles.summary: A looming fiscal reckoning could mean higher borrowing costs, taxes and everyday expenses. Financial planners share five moves to help keep your money on sol...
articles.body:
Billionaire Ray Dalio warned last week that the U.S. is heading for a major debt crisis, likening the nation to a person on the verge of a heart attack.

The Bridgewater Associates founder wrote in an August 21 LinkedIn post that a $4 billion U.S. debt buyback , combined with rising bond yields , a weak dollar and a Japanese sell-off of U.S. bond holdings all point to a potential government debt crisis, which can result in "the equivalent of an economic heart attack that comes when the constriction of debt-financed spending shuts down the normal flow of the economic circulatory system."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Dalio wrote that the U.S. will see around a $2 trillion budget shortfall this year, with $11 trillion in debt service payments. Earlier this month the U.S. topped $40 trillion in debt for the first time.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point because, if this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma," Dalio explained.

Otherwise, he added, the economic heart attack could come at any time, "hastened or postponed by policies and exogenous factors, like big political shifts and wars.

"My guess," he added, "is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

The debt clock is ticking — and the consequences could hit your wallet

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that, for 2026, the deficit will account for about 6% of the U.S. GDP, or $1.9 trillion.

Dalio proposed getting the budget deficit to 3% of the GDP by slashing spending, lowering interest rates and boosting tax revenue — strategies that he says "need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large" and causing a "traumatic" adjustment.

He cautioned, though, that "good fundamental adjustments" rather than a forced approach, like the Fed pushing interest rates down "unnaturally," are key.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, however, claimed that the U.S. budget deficit has peaked under President Trump and that "We can grow our way out" of the $40 trillion debt.

Dalio proposed getting the budget deficit to 3% of the GDP by slashing spending, lowering interest rates and boosting tax revenue — strategies that he says "need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large" and causing a "traumatic" adjustment.
He cautioned, though, that "good fundamental adjustments" rather than a forced approach, like the Fed pushing interest rates down "unnaturally," are key.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, however, claimed that the U.S. budget deficit has peaked under President Trump and that "We can grow our way out" of the $40 trillion debt.

articles.title: 2 measles-related deaths reported in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Two Pennsylvanians have died after contracting measles, the state’s health department said Tuesday. Both people, who were unvaccinated, lived in Lancaster County. The state health department said in a release it will not identify the deceased to protect their privacy and that of their families. Their deaths marked the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in…
articles.body:
Two Pennsylvanians have died after contracting measles, the state’s health department said Tuesday.

Both people, who were unvaccinated, lived in Lancaster County. The state health department said in a release it will not identify the deceased to protect their privacy and that of their families.

Their deaths marked the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in 35 years and the first in the country this year.

The U.S. has now seen five measles deaths in the last two years, more than the combined total of reported deaths over the past three decades.

During a press conference Tuesday, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) blamed misinformation for declining vaccination rates — specifically calling out the Trump administration.

“When the information we see coming from the federal government, in some cases, isn’t driven by facts and by science, it makes it even more confusing for parents, and that has a serious impact,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, widely seen as a Democratic presidential contender in 2028, added that he spoke with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. by phone on Tuesday about the two deaths.

“I was very, very blunt with him, and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said.

“There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids,” he continued.

Shapiro said he declined Kennedy’s offer of federal staffers to help with the outbreak.

Debra Bogen, the state’s health secretary, said her “deepest sympathies” are with the loved ones of the two deceased Pennsylvanians.

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Bogen said in a release. “We want to ensure every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities.”

The state health department noted it has confirmed 393 cases in 28 counties so far this year. Public health officials have confirmed 2,777 cases in the U.S. as of Thursday, with 94 percent of those cases associated with 36 outbreaks, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a statement co-signed by the CDC and its governing body, the Health and Human Services Department, the agency wrote that it is “working closely with state and local health departments to strengthen response efforts, rapidly support affected communities across the state, and communicate the steps people can take to slow the spread of measles.”

“The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread. CDC will continue to follow Pennsylvania’s lead and provide resources to support the state’s response,” the statement continued.

Bogen noted the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.”

Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order that proposes splitting up the MMR vaccine for children. The combined shot has been available since 1971, and doctors recommend kids receive it twice: at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years.

On the day he signed the order, Trump said the MMR vaccine was “lethal” in some cases, contradicting established medical consensus.

“Together there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” the president said in the Oval Office. “And separately it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.”

The heads of multiple medical groups, including the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics , have pushed back on Trump’s order — which also called for reducing the number of core vaccinations every child should receive to 11. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, also noted on Sunday that the MMR vaccine is not lethal.

This story was updated at 4:42 p.m. on Aug. 25, 2026.

articles.title: Gavin Newsom slams $20B of tariffs on Canadian goods, calls Canada 'our closest ally'
articles.summary: Reactions to the new tariffs have been fiery on both sides of the border, with California’s governor going so far as to use an expletive in a social media po...
articles.body:
The Canada-U.S. trade war has heated up again, after negotiations fell apart on Aug. 21, shortly before a deadline that established new, 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian exports.

Reactions to the new tariffs have been fiery on both sides of the border.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

California Governor Gavin Newsom's blistering response to the tariffs, for one, was unfiltered to say the least.

On Aug. 22, Newson made a post on social media platform X that said, "Our closest ally. Our critical trading partner. And Trump is hitting Canada with 50% tariffs. What the actual f— are we doing ?"

The trade war with Canada began as President Donald Trump started his second term, with Trump stating on his first day in office that he planned to levy 25% tariffs on Canada .

Since then, the U.S. has levied tariffs on goods that aren't compliant with the U.S.-Mexico Canada Agreement, as well as on imports such as steel and aluminum, and Canada has responded with counter-tariffs.

The most recent trade talks, which collapsed on Aug. 21, had been to "stave off punishing new tariffs by the Trump administration on Canadian goods," the New York Times reported .

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said he ceased the talks after the U.S. introduced terms at the last-minute that he said were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," the Times report says.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that "Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week, despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market," according to the Times.

"New demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said.

President Trump has, since the trade standoff began in 2025, made remarks threatening Canada's sovereignty, referring to it as " the 51st state ," and repeatedly referring to the prime minister as " governor ."

articles.title: Study suggests at least 25 percent of NFL players get CTE
articles.summary: A Tuesday report found that at least 25 percent of deceased NFL players who were studied suffered from chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in their lives. A team of researchers published a report in the British Medical Journal analyzing the brains of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Over the last six years…
articles.body:
A Tuesday report found that at least 25 percent of deceased NFL players who were studied suffered from chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in their lives.

A team of researchers published a report in the British Medical Journal analyzing the brains of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021.

Over the last six years of the study, researchers received 235 brains of the 878 NFL players who died. In that sample, 215 brains — 24.5 percent — were diagnosed with CTE. They estimated the prevalence of the disease could be far higher in those years as researchers were unable to analyze the other 643 brains that were not donated.

“The possible prevalence at death [of CTE] during 2016 to 2021, when brain donation was most frequent, ranged between 24.5 percent and 97.7 percent,” they wrote.

The study also noted that late-stage CTE is more prevalent in donors with dementia as research continues to trace the exact causes of the disease.

Another 2017 study in the Journal of American Medical Association reported similar results in the brains of 111 deceased NFL players; all but one were found to have CTE in the study.

The Mayo Clinic calls CTE a brain disease that can likely be caused by repeated head trauma and can cause emotional distress, mood swings and impact an individual’s behavior. The only way to be diagnosed with the disease is posthumously during a brain autopsy.

It outlined that CTE “appears to be related to repeated head injuries, often occurring in contact sports or military combat.”

The league most notably faced criticism when former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland was diagnosed with the condition after dying by suicide in 2025.

Researchers at Boston University also found that former New England Patriots player Aaron Hernandez, who died by suicide at 27, had the worst case of CTE seen in a young person, with his brain resembling that of a 60 year old.

The NFL Players Association, in a statement to ESPN , said that the study was “a sobering reminder that football carries real risks, and those risks can have lasting consequences for players and their families.”

“The findings should serve as a call to action across the entire football ecosystem. We all share a responsibility to advance research, improve access to care, develop better treatments, and support those affected by the long-term impacts of the game,” the association continued.

According to the British Medical Journal, 1,712 former NFL players died between 2008 and 2021, with 338 brains donated for research.

articles.title: Thyroid tablets recalled nationwide over potential ‘superpotency’: FDA
articles.summary: Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Vitruvias Therapeutics is voluntarily recalling one lot of thyroid tablet s because they could potentially be “superpotent,” federal regulators announced this week.

The high potency 30mg tablets could cause hyperthyroidism, or an overactive thyroid, according to the Food and Drug Administration . The affected lot (504950) was distributed nationwide to Vitruvias Therapeutics’ direct accounts from Jan. 31 to Sept. 30, 2025.

Consuming the recalled tablets could result in “weight loss, heat intolerance, fatigue, nervousness, muscle weakness, hypertension, chest pain, rapid heart rate, or heart rhythm disturbances,” the FDA warned. The elderly, pregnant women and infants are at the greatest risk.

Of the 3,655 units released, only 1955 were sold, the agency added.

Vitruvias Therapeutics is currently notifying wholesalers to stop distributing the recalled product and to arrange for its destruction.

The company hasn’t received any reports of negative impacts from the recalled tablets, which are used to treat hypothyroidism, or an underactive thyroid, the FDA added. Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.

For questions, consumers can contact Vitruvias Therapeutics by email at safety@vitruvias.com or by phone at (256) 239-9373 during standard business hours.

articles.title: Polestar claims it was blindsided by sales ban
articles.summary: Polestar thought it would be approved to continue selling its EVs in the US, and was blindsided by the Trump administration’s rejection of its application.
articles.body: Polestar said the Trump administration strung it along for months before finally rejecting its request to continue selling its electric vehicles in the US under a rule outlawing vehicles with connected software from China. In an August 18th letter sent to dealers and obtained by The Verge, Polestar said it doesn’t have a clear answer as to why its application to continue selling its EVs in the US was denied, considering its sister company Volvo was authorized to sell its vehicles despite similar corporate ownership. (The letter was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.) The US Department of Commerce approved Volvo in May 2026 to continue importing and selling its vehicles in the US, despite restrictions tied to its majority Chinese owner, Geely. But one month later, the department rejected Polestar’s similar request, leading to the company to announce it would stop selling its vehicles in the US starting with the 2027 model year. The rule, which originated under the Biden administration, bans the import and sale of vehicles with connected software from hostile countries, including China. In the letter to dealers, Polestar’s head of product Peter Wexler lays out the timeline of the company’s communications with the Trump administration, starting with a May 29, 2025 application to the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Commerce Department. In subsequent meetings, Wexler says Polestar was given the impression that Polestar would be approved, considering its vehicles are functionally similar to Volvo’s. Jeffrey Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, said during an in-person meeting with Polestar’s representatives “that it would be reasonable for Polestar to expect approval of its applications if Volvo Cars was approved to sell its cars under effectively the same shareholding and ownership structure and with the same hardware and software in the Polestar 3 as the Volvo EX90,” Wexler writes. Polestar told the administration it open to a variety of “mitigation measures” to ensure its vehicles were compliant with the ban on Chinese software, including regular audits, geographic restrictions on data storage and management, and limitations on digital keys and remote access. But the administration declined all such offers, Wexler said. “BIS never engaged in any such discussions with Polestar,” he writes. “Instead, BIS communicated that it had all the information it required to render a decision.” Wexler said that Polestar is continuing to press the administration for an explanation on why it was denied approval. The company was sued recently by Polestar dealer Prestige Imports in New Jersey, which accuses the company of engineering its own exit from the US by failing to do enough to satisfy regulators at the Commerce Department.

articles.title: 9/11 victim identified nearly 25 years later with new forensic technique
articles.summary: The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City.
articles.body:
NEW YORK ( WPIX ) — As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks approaches, a victim has been identified, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday.

The adult woman was identified using a breakthrough technique of forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG.

She is the first 9/11 victim identified using the technique and the 1,654th victim identified through analysis of remains recovered from the attacks, according to officials. The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City.

“As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific Sept. 11 attacks, we honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day, and we remain committed to the families who have spent 25 years waiting for answers,” Mamdani said.

“The identification of this victim through forensic investigative genetic genealogy is a powerful example of what is possible when we pair cutting-edge technology with an unwavering commitment to those we lost,” the mayor added.

FIGG pairs specialized DNA technologies with genealogical investigative techniques to produce leads in identifying victims. They are then confirmed through the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner through DNA and other forensic methods.

The name of the victim is being withheld at the request of the family.

Before Monday, the last time a victim of the 9/11 attacks at the World Trade Center was identified was in August 2025.

articles.title: What is CTE, and how many former NFL players have been diagnosed with it?
articles.summary: So far, the degenerative brain disease has only been diagnosed after a person’s death.
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org .

(NEXSTAR) – A new study led by researchers out of Massachusetts suggests that among those who have played in the NFL, at least one in four may develop chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease that carries no cure and has only been diagnosed after death.

The study , published in The BMJ, reviewed the hundreds of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Of the more than 1,700 who died, researchers reported that the brains of 338 were studied. Postmortem brain analysis has, so far, been the only proven method of determining whether someone has CTE, a degenerative brain disease.

Of the 338 brains that were studied, it was determined that 315 donors had a CTE diagnosis.

Among players who died within the last six years – a time in which “brain donation was more frequent” – researchers said 235 NFL players donated their brains for analysis. More than 210 were found to have CTE.

Just over 200 of the 338 whose brains were analyzed had been previously diagnosed with dementia. The study found that donors with dementia were later found to have more severe cases of CTE: 94 had Stage 4 CTE, considered the most severe level.

Broadly speaking, CTE impacts how the brain functions. Research has suggested that CTE is “linked to a build-up of abnormal proteins that damage brain tissue and cause brain cells to undergo cell death,” the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains .

CTE is often found in people who have experienced repeated impacts to the head, making football players among the most commonly associated with the disease. However, as the Boston University CTE Center notes , the condition has been linked to boxers and soccer and hockey players, as well as those who have served in the military or as first responders. Even athletes who stopped participating in sports in high school and college have been diagnosed with CTE.

Symptoms can take years or decades to develop, experts say. When they do appear, they can last for months or years. The exact symptoms associated with CTE are unclear, but the CDC explains that those who are diagnosed are later described as having “problems with thinking, emotions, mood, suicidal thoughts and/or behaviors that became serious enough to get in the way of normal daily activities.”

“However, having these symptoms does not necessarily mean a person has CTE,” the CDC adds. “It is important to talk to a doctor if you, a family member, or friend have any questions or concerns. Treatments are available to help with many of these symptoms.”

Research to better understand CTE – including how it develops, what risk factors may be associated with it, and how to diagnose it earlier – continues, according to Boston University.

Hundreds of NFL players diagnosed with CTE after death

As the latest study found, there have been hundreds of NFL players who, after their brains were studied following their deaths, were diagnosed with CTE. (A 2023 report said that of the 376 former NFL players studied by Boston University’s CTE Center, 345 had been diagnosed with the brain disease.)

Among the most recently diagnosed was former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland , who died by suicide in November following a high-speed chase with police. Boston University researchers analyzed Kneeland’s brain tissue and determined he had Stage 1 CTE.

Aaron Hernandez , whose 2017 death was ruled a suicide, was found to have Stage 3 CTE. He had been in prison at the time of his death in a murder case.

Former Tennessee Titan Frank Wycheck , who died in 2023 after apparently hitting his head in a fall at home, had Stage 3 CTE, his family said. Former NFL Pro Bowl wide receiver Demaryius Thomas had been dealing with depression, anxiety and other CTE symptoms at the time of his 2021 death. His family later confirmed he had Stage 2 CTE.

Irv Cross , a former NFL player turned CBS anchor, was found to have had CTE following his 2021 death. His widow, Liz Cross, told the Associated Press in 2023 that the former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback had experienced depression, mood swings and memory loss that made him not “want to be with people.” Boston University researchers determined Cross had Stage 4 CTE .

Phillip Adams , who spent several seasons in the NFL, fatally shot six people in Rock Hill, South Carolina, before killing himself in 2021. An autopsy later showed he had Stage 2 CTE , Nexstar’s WJZY reported.

Shane Tamura, the man who killed four people in the same New York City building that houses the NFL’s headquarters, was found to have CTE . In a note found on his body, Tamura expressed a grievance with the league – he played football, but never in the NFL – and claimed he suffered from CTE.

paragraphs: Editor’s Note: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org .

(NEXSTAR) – A new study led by researchers out of Massachusetts suggests that among those who have played in the NFL, at least one in four may develop chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease that carries no cure and has only been diagnosed after death.

The study , published in The BMJ, reviewed the hundreds of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Of the more than 1,700 who died, researchers reported that the brains of 338 were studied. Postmortem brain analysis has, so far, been the only proven method of determining whether someone has CTE, a degenerative brain disease.
Of the 338 brains that were studied, it was determined that 315 donors had a CTE diagnosis.

Among players who died within the last six years – a time in which “brain donation was more frequent” – researchers said 235 NFL players donated their brains for analysis. More than 210 were found to have CTE.

Just over 200 of the 338 whose brains were analyzed had been previously diagnosed with dementia. The study found that donors with dementia were later found to have more severe cases of CTE: 94 had Stage 4 CTE, considered the most severe level.

Broadly speaking, CTE impacts how the brain functions. Research has suggested that CTE is “linked to a build-up of abnormal proteins that damage brain tissue and cause brain cells to undergo cell death,” the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains .

CTE is often found in people who have experienced repeated impacts to the head, making football players among the most commonly associated with the disease. However, as the Boston University CTE Center notes , the condition has been linked to boxers and soccer and hockey players, as well as those who have served in the military or as first responders. Even athletes who stopped participating in sports in high school and college have been diagnosed with CTE.

Symptoms can take years or decades to develop, experts say. When they do appear, they can last for months or years. The exact symptoms associated with CTE are unclear, but the CDC explains that those who are diagnosed are later described as having “problems with thinking, emotions, mood, suicidal thoughts and/or behaviors that became serious enough to get in the way of normal daily activities.”

“However, having these symptoms does not necessarily mean a person has CTE,” the CDC adds. “It is important to talk to a doctor if you, a family member, or friend have any questions or concerns. Treatments are available to help with many of these symptoms.”
Research to better understand CTE – including how it develops, what risk factors may be associated with it, and how to diagnose it earlier – continues, according to Boston University.
Hundreds of NFL players diagnosed with CTE after death

As the latest study found, there have been hundreds of NFL players who, after their brains were studied following their deaths, were diagnosed with CTE. (A 2023 report said that of the 376 former NFL players studied by Boston University’s CTE Center, 345 had been diagnosed with the brain disease.)

Among the most recently diagnosed was former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland , who died by suicide in November following a high-speed chase with police. Boston University researchers analyzed Kneeland’s brain tissue and determined he had Stage 1 CTE.
Aaron Hernandez , whose 2017 death was ruled a suicide, was found to have Stage 3 CTE. He had been in prison at the time of his death in a murder case.

Former Tennessee Titan Frank Wycheck , who died in 2023 after apparently hitting his head in a fall at home, had Stage 3 CTE, his family said. Former NFL Pro Bowl wide receiver Demaryius Thomas had been dealing with depression, anxiety and other CTE symptoms at the time of his 2021 death. His family later confirmed he had Stage 2 CTE.

Irv Cross , a former NFL player turned CBS anchor, was found to have had CTE following his 2021 death. His widow, Liz Cross, told the Associated Press in 2023 that the former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback had experienced depression, mood swings and memory loss that made him not “want to be with people.” Boston University researchers determined Cross had Stage 4 CTE .

Phillip Adams , who spent several seasons in the NFL, fatally shot six people in Rock Hill, South Carolina, before killing himself in 2021. An autopsy later showed he had Stage 2 CTE , Nexstar’s WJZY reported.

Shane Tamura, the man who killed four people in the same New York City building that houses the NFL’s headquarters, was found to have CTE . In a note found on his body, Tamura expressed a grievance with the league – he played football, but never in the NFL – and claimed he suffered from CTE.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
