articles.title: Canada slaps retaliatory tariffs on US goods worth $20 billion as trade war intensifies
articles.summary: By Promit Mukherjee and Bhargav Acharya OTTAWA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Canada hit back on Tuesday with retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. ann...
articles.body:
OTTAWA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Canada hit back on Tuesday with retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. annual imports and rolled out aid for businesses and workers, matching Washington's latest ‌duties dollar-for-dollar.

The counter-tariffs on U.S. goods take effect on September 8 and impose duties of 15%, 25% and 50% ‌across around 700 products imported from south of the border, a government statement said.

U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect ​on Saturday after talks between the two countries collapsed.

The new tit-for-tat tariffs mark a new low in relations between the longtime allies, and Trump earlier on Tuesday threatened to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles both countries, "Lake America."

"Our dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs as well as a multi-billion dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Canada's Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said.

The White House and the U.S. ‌Trade Representative did not immediately respond to a ⁠request for comment.

Canada levied the 50% tariffs on steel, aluminum, furniture and clothing, set the 25% tariffs on cheese, appliances and some seafood, and placed the 15% tariffs on electronics and tools, a Canadian ⁠government official told reporters.

Trump's new tariffs are relatively narrow, affecting roughly 5% of Canada's exports to the United States. But trade analysts say they could have severe, concentrated effects on some sectors that are already struggling like wood products, particularly kitchen cabinet makers.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs, calculated using ​2024 ​trade figures, cover goods accounting for nearly 4.5% of Canada's imports from ​the United States.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly said the counter-tariffs ‌were primarily aimed at protecting Canadian businesses but were also aimed at applying political pressure before Americans vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

"We need to make sure that the competitors don't have access to the Canadian market in a better way than their own... products, and that's why the retailers need to show that from Canada," she said.

"Second, we're also targeting products that will target states in the U.S. and so we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure, and that's why we think it's ‌the right thing to do right now."

The Canadian tariffs will also cover some ​prepared foods, perfumes and toiletries, plastics, lumber, wood pulp and paper products, ​carpets and clothing.

articles.title: Paxton unveils data center plan, joining other GOP candidates in calling for restrictions
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan Monday to place restrictions on data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure. Paxton laid out his four-point plan, vowing to “fiercely advocate” for Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) state-level data center…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan Monday to place restrictions on data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure.

Paxton laid out his four-point plan, vowing to “fiercely advocate” for Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) state-level data center plan and sponsor or back various federal legislation.

This includes legislation that would bar the use of Chinese technology to power data centers and would hold data center developers criminally liable if their infrastructure “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”

He also said he would co-sponsor the Decentralized Access to Technology Alternatives Act, a bill from Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) that would exempt new, off-grid electricity providers from certain federal regulations in an effort to prevent data centers from raising consumer electricity costs.

“My Texas First Data Center Plan will protect our grid, our communities, and our children while ensuring America beats Communist China in the AI race,” Paxton wrote in a post on the social platform X. “Texas First. Always.”

Paxton is facing off against Democratic nominee James Talarico in a tight race for the Texas Senate seat, which the Cook Political Report recently classified as a “toss-up.”

Data centers have increasingly become a central issue in the midterm elections, as Americans have grown wary of the push to rapidly build more of the sprawling server warehouses to support AI development.

This has prompted several Republican candidates to stake out positions against data centers , even as President Trump continues to embrace the build-out.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced last week that he was calling for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction in the state.

In the Pennsylvania governor’s race, Republican Stacy Garrity is calling for a “pause” on data center development and has taken aim at incumbent Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) over his prior support for such projects.

Meanwhile, Abbott announced a series of new restrictions on data centers in June, directing the state’s utility and its regulator to take steps to limit economic impacts on residents. He also pledged to work with the Texas Legislature to mandate water-efficient technologies and repeal data center incentives.

Earlier this month, the Texas governor also said he was placing a moratorium on new data center approvals pending a state audit.

articles.title: Florida moves to end certain school vaccination requirements
articles.summary: The state of Florida wants to roll back a requirement that public and private school children receive four vaccines before enrolling. A proposed rule from the state’s Health Department would allow students to attend school and enroll in daycare without first receiving hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. …
articles.body:
The state of Florida wants to roll back a requirement that public and private school children receive four vaccines before enrolling.

A proposed rule from the state’s Health Department would allow students to attend school and enroll in daycare without first receiving hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.

The proposal would also broaden religious objections to vaccinations, allowing parents to opt-out for any moral or ethical beliefs. Parents and college students could also object to having their information shared with a statewide vaccination database.

Florida currently allows religious exemptions “if immunizations are in conflict with the religious tenets and practices of the child’s parent or guardian,” according to the state’s Health Department.

The proposal comes almost a year after Dr. Joseph Ladapo, Florida’s surgeon general, first announced his intent to eliminate vaccine requirements in the Sunshine State. He did not specify any specific vaccines at the time but said he would end “all of them.”

“Every last one of them is wrong and drips with disdain and slavery,” Ladapo, a longtime vaccine skeptic, said.

The proposed rule is not the first time the state has tried to loosen vaccine requirements.

Last month, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) warned private Catholic schools they needed to allow religious exemptions from vaccine requirements as required by state law, otherwise they could be disqualified from scholarships and vouchers.

“As a Catholic, I am confident that the teachings of the Catholic Church do not require Catholic schools to compel students to take vaccines derived from the tissue of aborted children,” Uthmeier wrote to the state’s Conference of Catholic Bishops.

In a letter to Uthmeier dated Aug. 7, the bishops made it clear there is no religious reason for parents to opt out of vaccinating their children.

Their position is rooted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, which states that “life and physical health are precious gifts entrusted to us by God.”

The bishops told Uthmeier they are the ones who decide how to interpret Catholic principles and theology, not the government. Attempting to force the schools to adopt the government’s position is a violation of their religious liberty.

“Any insinuation that a government official can dictate to the Catholic Church (or any religion) how to apply her tenets and dogma, violates well-established constitutional religious freedom rights,” wrote Michael B. Sheedy, the organization’s executive director.

“We are prepared to protect our students, defend our rights, and preserve religious freedom,” he wrote.

By law, Florida requires students be vaccinated against polio, diphtheria, measles, rubella, pertussis, mumps, tetanus “and other communicable diseases as determined by rules of the Department of Health.”

The vaccines in question were required under the Health Department’s rule, so the agency is attempting another rule to change the requirement. The requirements for the other vaccines would need to be changed by the Legislature, and no bills have been introduced to do so.

The proposed rule was published Monday and is open for public comment through Sept. 14.

It was released one day after Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the state’s GOP gubernatorial candidate, said on “Face the Nation” he’d like to “study” and “really engage” before making a decision about school requirements for polio and measles.

The U.S. has recorded the most measles infections in 35 years, amid declining vaccination rates. Florida has 142 reported measles cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

When more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated against measles, most people are protected through herd immunity. Florida has only an 88.9 percent vaccination rate, according to CDC data.

In the same interview Sunday, Donalds also claimed without evidence the reason for the surge in measles in certain parts of the country is because of “rampant illegal immigration.”

Florida’s moves come as the Trump administration seeks to overhaul the childhood vaccine schedule to reduce and space out recommended childhood vaccines — an effort that most pediatricians have decried as dangerous.

Physicians and other health experts have long supported school vaccination requirements as a way of stopping the spread of infectious diseases among children and their communities by contributing to herd immunity.

When asked about Florida’s plan to roll back the requirements last year, President Trump told reporters that some vaccines “ just pure and simple work .”

“I think we have to be very careful. You have some vaccines that are so amazing,” Trump said, citing the polio vaccine and the COVID-19 vaccine, which was developed during his first term.

articles.title: Four Fed bank boards wanted rate hike, minutes show
articles.summary: By Ann Saphir Aug 25 (Reuters) - Directors at four of the Federal Reserve's 12 banks voted to increase the interest rate charged to commercial banks for emer...
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - Directors at four of the Federal Reserve's 12 banks voted to ‌increase the interest rate charged to commercial banks for ‌emergency loans in the days before the U.S. central bank's July ​meeting, minutes of the central bank's discount rate meetings released on Tuesday, showed.

The rate recommendations, overruled when Fed policymakers decided in a 9-3 vote to leave the policy rate ‌unchanged at their ⁠July 28 to 29 meeting, provide a fresh window into how contested that decision was.

Voting ⁠for a primary credit rate increase of a quarter of a percentage point were the directors of the three ​banks that ​had dissented at the July ​meeting -- Dallas, Cleveland and ‌Minneapolis Fed -- plus the board at the Kansas City Fed, whose president, Jeff Schmid, does not have a vote this year on the policy rate.

Fed bank directors are not policymakers and do not determine the Fed's interest ‌rate, but they do meet regularly ​with their respective Fed presidents ​who say their directors' ​views help shape their own outlooks.

Regional Fed ‌bank boards vote on the ​discount rate at ​regular meetings, but it is ultimately set by the Fed Board to match the top of the ​range of the ‌policy target rate, which has been in the ​3.5% to 3.75% range since December.

(Reporting by Ann ​Saphi; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

articles.title: Wisconsin district attorney declines to charge Musk over $1M voter giveaway
articles.summary: A Wisconsin state prosecutor declined to charge technology billionaire Elon Musk with election bribery for his $1 million check handouts to voters during the state’s Supreme Court election last year. In a letter shared Tuesday with The Hill, La Crosse County District Attorney Tim Gruenke (D) said his office decided against pressing charges since, in…
articles.body:
A Wisconsin state prosecutor declined to charge technology billionaire Elon Musk with election bribery for his $1 million check handouts to voters during the state’s Supreme Court election last year.

In a letter shared Tuesday with The Hill, La Crosse County District Attorney Tim Gruenke (D) said his office decided against pressing charges since, in the end, “nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote.”

Musk, the CEO and founder of Tesla and SpaceX, initially announced in March 2025 that he would speak in Wisconsin, with entrance limited to those who had voted in the state’s Supreme Court election.

Musk said on his social platform X he would “personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote.”

About 12 hours later, the post was deleted and replaced with another clarifying entrance was limited to those who signed the petition against “activist judges.” He said the money would be given to “spokesmen” for the petition.

Musk went on to hand out two checks during a campaign rally in Wisconsin.

Gruenke argued the first post could be seen as an offer to pay someone “the possibility of winning a lottery at a town hall by voting,” but could also be seen as giving entry to a free town hall, with the money a “pre-determined payment for people selected as ‘spokesman’ rather than a reward for voting.”

“Under either view, the second post apparently recognized that potential violation and corrected it,” Gruenke wrote.

“Even if I could convince a jury that the original post was still a bribe, I do not believe that a jury would convict Elon Musk of a crime after considering the intent, the second post, and the fact nothing of value was ever given to anyone for voting for an incident occurring in March of 2025,” he added.

Gruenke’s decision comes about a month after the bipartisan elections panel voted 5-1 to refer two complaints against Musk to the Brown County, Wis., district attorney’s office. The panel, which has three Democrats and three Republicans, found probable cause that the giveaways violated the state’s election bribery law.

Gruenke was appointed as a special prosecutor because of a conflict of interest.

Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul (D) sued Musk over the giveaway later that month. The lower court declined to block the giveaways as an illegal bribe to voters, prompting Kaul to ask the state’s top court to stop the check handouts.

But Gruenke concluded that without “the famous name” and large dollar figures involved, the incident was a “simple case of a poorly worded statement that was corrected and brought into compliance with the law.”

Musk’s legal team did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Despite Musk’s efforts, the conservative candidate he backed, Brad Schimel, lost to Democratic-backed Susan Crawford, keeping the high court’s liberal majority.

articles.title: CIA director makes unannounced visit to Russia
articles.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, CBS News reported. Flight trackers spotted a U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane flying from Riga, Latvia, to Moscow on Tuesday. The CIA and the White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request…
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, CBS News reported .

Flight trackers spotted a U.S. Air Force Boeing C-17A Globemaster III transport plane flying from Riga, Latvia, to Moscow on Tuesday.

The CIA and the White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The visit is Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia since being confirmed as the CIA director in early 2025.

Ahead of Ratcliffe’s visit, the Trump administration asked Ukrainian officials last week not to strike Moscow, St. Petersburg and northern regions of the country with its long-range drones and missiles Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, as the U.S. would dispatch a senior official to Moscow, the Financial Times reported .

Ratcliffe’s plane was spotted departing Moscow around noon, according to flight-tracking data.

Recent U.S. intelligence reports posited that Russian President Vladimir Putin could attempt to test NATO with a limited assault on a member nation in the next few years, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month.

Ratcliffe’s visit also comes as the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine to end the war in eastern Europe appear to be stalled.

Former CIA Director William Burns traveled to Russia in November 2021, during which he met with Russian officials and warned Putin against invading Ukraine.

articles.title: Army sergeant’s wife deported to Honduras under Trump crackdown
articles.summary: The wife of an active-duty U.S. soldier has reportedly been deported to Honduras, her native country, in the latest instance of a family member of an American service member being swept up in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Multiple outlets reported that Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez and…
articles.body:
The wife of an active-duty U.S. soldier has reportedly been deported to Honduras, her native country, in the latest instance of a family member of an American service member being swept up in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Multiple outlets reported that Cristy Maryori Villafranca-Trejo, the wife of Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez and mother of their 6-year-old daughter, was deported Monday. She had left Honduras in 2016 due to violent crime in the country, according to her husband.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Villafranca-Trejo had “received due process” ahead of her deportation.

She is at least the seventh spouse or parent of an active-duty military member to be removed from the country, with more than 50 cases of immediate family of American troops, sailors and airmen placed in federal immigration detention, according to The Associated Press .

Military family members were largely seen as safe from deportations until President Trump’s second term, when protections were rolled back.

Turcios Juarez previously told ABC News that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detained Villafranca-Trejo July 11 outside of a Walmart in Fort Bliss, Texas, in front of their daughter.

The Army sergeant has since told The Associated Press he has been struggling to manage his military duties since his wife was detained as he has had to care for their child without her help, skipping training in the mornings to take his daughter to school. He also told the outlet he has had to postpone a planned assignment at another base.

“I don’t know if I will be able to continue with this,” Turcios Juarez told the AP of his service. “I have to make a plan to make sure I can still fulfill my military responsibilities — but also take care of my family.”

Villafranca-Trejo entered the U.S. when she was 18 years old and has no known criminal record but was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge in 2017 after failing to appear at a hearing, DHS told the outlet.

But her husband said she had not received a notice for the hearing and didn’t know she had been ordered deportation until 2022, when they went to apply for her green card after marrying.

Turcios Juarez, also originally from Honduras, became a U.S. citizen in 2024 after enlisting in 2022.

Villafranca-Trejo had been waiting for roughly a year to see if her application for military parole-in-place — which allows the immediate family of U.S. troops to remain in the country to apply for a green card — was approved.

“We were following the rules, we did everything we could on our side to fix this problem,” Turcios Juarez told the AP.

Villafranca-Trejo’s removal comes as a Navy sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln — the aircraft carrier that has received attention in recent weeks due to its extended deployment in the Middle East coupled with reports of poor conditions and low morale among its services members — posted to social media that his father had been detained by U.S. immigration authorities this week.

Sailor Joshua Aviles said his 48-year-old father Luis Manuel Aviles had a driver’s license, Social Security card and a permit to work in the U.S., and was waiting to get his green card approved.

“We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting,” Aviles wrote on Facebook .

“This is heartbreaking for me. I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal,” he continued.

“My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”

articles.title: Senate Democrats question RFK Jr. on vaccine settlement divestment
articles.summary: Several Senate Democrats are questioning whether Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. truly divested his financial interests in a lawsuit he helped spearhead challenging the HPV vaccine Gardasil. Before he was confirmed as HHS secretary, Kennedy was part of a lawsuit led by the firm Wisner Baum against the pharmaceutical company…
articles.body:
Several Senate Democrats are questioning whether Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. truly divested his financial interests in a lawsuit he helped spearhead challenging the HPV vaccine Gardasil.

Before he was confirmed as HHS secretary, Kennedy was part of a lawsuit led by the firm Wisner Baum against the pharmaceutical company Merck, alleging that its HPV vaccine Gardasil caused neurological and autoimmune injuries.

During his confirmation process, Kennedy assured senators that he would divest his financial interests in the lawsuit, though he had initially indicated plans to retain part of the fees awarded in the case, arguing at the time that he was “entitled” to that money and wasn’t actively involved in the case as an attorney.

“An amendment to my Ethics Agreement is in process. It provides that I will divest my interest in any such litigation via an assignment to my non-dependent, adult son,” Kennedy wrote in a letter to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) at the time.

Led by Warren, fellow Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden (Ore.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Angela Alsobrooks (Md.) questioned whether he stuck to this commitment.

In their letter to Kennedy, Warren wrote, “My staff has conducted a diligent review of all of your public financial disclosures and ethics documents and have identified no amendments or modifications to any of these materials. Nor has the Senate Finance Committee identified any information indicating you have changed the disposition of your Gardasil stake.”

The senators demanded to know whether Kennedy had transferred his stake in the lawsuit to a nondependent adult child, as he had said he would, or if he had transferred it to Wisner Baum.

Merck agreed to pay $50 million earlier this year to settle the lawsuit without admitting any guilt and maintained that its product was safe and effective. Gardasil first received approval in 2006 for female patients before getting expanded approval for male patients in 2009.

The lawmakers asked to know what fees he would stand to receive from the settlement.

The Hill has reached out to the HHS for comment on the inquiry.

When reached for comment, Wisner Baum said in a statement. “Neither Secretary Kennedy nor his son have received any fees from any alleged settlement with Merck related to Gardasil. At no time will either receive any fees from the alleged Gardasil settlement.”

articles.title: TSA ditches Gold+ privatized airport security program
articles.summary: The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced Monday it will phase out its new Gold+ private airport screening program, opting instead to optimize its existing Screening Partnership Program (SPP). TSA unveiled the change as part of its Horizon 25 Strategy, named in honor of the agency’s 25th anniversary. The strategy will home in on modernizing TSA…
articles.body:
The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) announced Monday it will phase out its new Gold+ private airport screening program, opting instead to optimize its existing Screening Partnership Program (SPP).

TSA unveiled the change as part of its Horizon 25 Strategy, named in honor of the agency’s 25th anniversary. The strategy will home in on modernizing TSA checkpoints, elevating the traveler experience and hardening multimodal transportation security, the agency noted.

TSA launched the Gold+ program earlier this year, allowing airports to enter partnerships with private contractors to handle their security and screening operations. Agency officials said private security firms would be able to tailor security measures for individual airports, while complying with overarching federal standards.

But TSA is shelving the short-lived initiative in favor of an “evolved” SPP, through which 20 airports outsource screening services to private companies — with the federal agency overseeing operations.

Kansas City International Airport, Orlando Sanford International Airport and San Francisco International Airport are among the airports participating in the public-private program, according to TSA .

The agency noted Tuesday the evolved SPP will “better harness the role of the private sector in delivering a safer, more secure, and more efficient aviation system.”

TSA Administrator David Cummins, whom the GOP-controlled Senate confirmed to the post last month, said President Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have entrusted him “with the task of modernizing” the security-focused agency.

“In its first 25 years, this agency has performed its critical Homeland Security mission with dedication and excellence,” Cummins said in the release. The new TSA administrator has experience in the private sector, and was the director of operations management for the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City, Utah.

“As we look forward to the next 25 years, we must constantly work to stay ahead of evolving threats and deliver a Golden Age of Travel,” Cummins added. “Through the Horizon 25 Strategy, we will build a TSA that is agile, resilient and ready for tomorrow’s challenges.”

He later said, “TSA does not have to choose between a secure checkpoint, an efficient checkpoint, and an elevated passenger experience. Through Horizon 25, TSA can, and will, deliver all three at once.”

While the Gold+ program required vendors to provide their own screening equipment, private screening vendors at airports enrolled in the SPP must utilize TSA equipment. The agency’s federal security director is still in charge of security, incident management and stakeholder relations, TSA notes .

Tampa International Airport, after conducting a review of the Gold+ program, said Monday it had elected to keep screening operations “exclusively” with the TSA. That garnered praise from Everett Kelley, the president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union representing 47,000 TSA officers.

“TSA Gold+ is a major departure from our country’s current aviation screening security system, which has kept the flying public safe for nearly 25 years and should be applauded instead of abandoned,” Kelley said in an AFGE release . “Tampa airport officials made the right call, and I hope other airports thinking of privatizing their security functions will follow suit and stay with TSA.”

The government union filed a lawsuit earlier this month to compel TSA to turn over records related to the since-spiked program, which it accused the agency of developing and promoting to contractors “quietly” without notifying employees, congressional lawmakers or airport authorities.

During the record-long government shutdown last fall, TSA employees went weeks without pay, with call-out rates soaring and more than 1,000 agency officers leaving the force entirely.

That sparked an increase in airport security wait times across the country, with the situation repeating itself this past winter and spring during a 76-day shutdown of the Homeland Security Department.

articles.title: Pennsylvania attorney general accuses Snapchat of failing to protect children in new lawsuit
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday (R) announced a lawsuit Tuesday, accusing Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, of failing to protect children from compulsively using its platform. The complaint, filed this week, alleges Snapchat knowingly lies about the frequency of adult-themed material like drug use or sexual content to maintain a 13+ app rating in…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday (R) announced a lawsuit Tuesday, accusing Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, of failing to protect children from compulsively using its platform.

The complaint , filed this week, alleges Snapchat knowingly lies about the frequency of adult-themed material like drug use or sexual content to maintain a 13+ app rating in app stores.

“Once they have you signed up and logged in, you are officially in their clutches,” the attorney general said at a press conference Tuesday. “From there, Snapchat essentially says good luck getting out.”

Sunday said he hopes for “honesty” from Snapchat, accusing the company’s actions of violating Pennsylvania’s consumer protection laws.

“The lawsuit also demands that Snapchat finally come clean about the addictiveness of their app and takes real action to protect young users,” Sunday said. “This is a very serious legal action with the end goals of being an overhaul of how Snapchat markets and advertises its app.”

Sunday alleged Snapchat uses functions like the Snap Streak feature, which counts the number of days two users send Snaps to one another to keep users engaged. The streak is lost when one of the users does not Snap the other in 24 hours.

“We allege this streak feature puts a tangible value on friendships and influences a child’s feelings of self-worth,” he said.

Sunday also argued that Snapchat’s disappearing stories, messages and photos encourage users to post things they may typically not, like a revealing selfie.

The state prosecutor said parents do not have time to “fully explore” every platform and relies on “transparency” from companies when making decisions about their children’s social media use.

A spokesperson for Snap stated that the allegations “fundamentally misrepresent” the platform and its approach to teen safety.

“Snapchat was designed differently from the beginning: it opens to a camera, not a feed of content, and was built to encourage self-expression and authentic connection with friends,” the spokesperson told The Hill.

“We share the Attorney General’s commitment to protecting young people online and are disappointed they have chosen litigation rather than working with us toward that shared goal,” the spokesperson continued.

Sunday’s suit comes just weeks after he announced a complaint against TikTok over similar allegations .

articles.title: Internal watchdog finds FEMA crew violated Hatch Act by skipping homes with Trump signs
articles.summary: A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in 2024, according to an internal government watchdog. A new report from the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general’s office determined that the crew violated the Hatch Act and FEMA policy when it skipped…
articles.body:
A Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) crew broke the law when it skipped houses with President Trump signs during Hurricane Milton recovery efforts in 2024, according to an internal government watchdog.

A new report from the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general’s office determined that the crew violated the Hatch Act and FEMA policy when it skipped 11 Florida homes that indicated support for Trump, who was a candidate at the time.

It said that the incident “eroded public trust in FEMA’s ability to treat everyone impartially, offer unbiased and consistent assistance, and ensure equal access to resources and tools.”

The report blamed “weaknesses in FEMA’s training, documentation, and oversight,” saying that the agency did give crews ethics and Hatch Act training before responding to disasters.

The incident became a political flash point at the time and stoked significant GOP scrutiny of the disaster response agency. Trump eventually called for abolishing FEMA, though he later pivoted for trying to downsize it and limit aid given to states.

The Office of the Special Counsel similarly found last year that the incident in question violated the Hatch Act. A spokesperson for the inspector general’s office confirmed that the new report pertains to the same incident.

The Hatch Act limits federal employees’ political activities while acting in their official capacity, including barring them from using their official authority to influence election results.

Christopher Logan, FEMA’s associate administrator, said that the agency no longer conducts “FEMA-led door-to-door outreach efforts.”

“Staff now provide support to survivors from fixed locations determined by state and local officials through a data-informed approach,” Logan wrote in an official response to the report.

He also said that after the incident, the agency gave Disaster Survivor Assistance crews mandatory Hatch Act and ethics training.

Michael Coen, who was FEMA’s chief of staff during the Biden administration, said in a text message to The Hill that the report “reinforces” that the “violations were not systematic and were isolated.”

“FEMA took appropriate action when the violations were briefed to senior leadership,” Coen said.

The inspector general’s report also notes that the office could not determine if crews skipped locations for reasons that were not allowed during other disasters because then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem did not act on FEMA’s request to fund the agency’s field assessment and collection tools.

The report comes after the Trump administration itself has also faced accusations of politicizing disaster aid. Politico reported earlier this year that the president had approved 23 percent of disaster funding requests from blue states and 89 percent of requests from red states.

articles.title: US launches new drug boat strike in the Caribbean, citing narcoterrorism
articles.summary: The U.S. military launched a lethal strike on Tuesday against an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean traveling through “established narco-trafficking routes” as outlined by Southern Command. articles.body:
The U.S. military launched a lethal strike on Tuesday against an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean traveling through “established narco-trafficking routes” as outlined by Southern Command.

Four onboard the vessel were killed. It follows a Monday attack on an alleged drug boat in the Eastern Pacific in which two people were killed.

Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan ordered the Tuesday attack based on “confirmed intelligence” that “revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking,” read an update from Southcom.

It’s at least the 68th attack launched by alleged drug traffickers sailing in the Caribbean.

“We will hunt, disrupt, and defeat these narco-terrorist networks,” Francis said in a statement on the matter.

“SOUTHCOM is resolved to neutralizing cartel terror and violence throughout the region and into the U.S. homeland,” he added.

Lawmakers have questioned the intelligence behind the strikes and foreign leaders from Colombia and Venezuela have concluded citizens killed onboard the vessels were not gang members involved in the transnational sale of narcotics.

The Trump administration denied those claims and has declared several gangs ranging from Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua and the Mexican cartel known as the Jalisco New Generation Cartel to the Sinaloa Cartel as terrorist organizations.

The White House says the designation gives them free reign to strike those discovered to be connected to the entities as they aim to fight narcoterrorism and address the fentanyl crisis.

The illicitly manufactured synthetic opioid causes tens of thousands of overdose deaths annually across the U.S.
